  10. Interpret the results of regression analysis.

Introduction

We have covered the first three steps in the data mining process: data exploration, sampling, and modification. All these efforts prepare us for the most critical step in this process—modeling. In this step, researchers select machine learning methods, build and configure multiple models, train the models with data, and validate them. The outcome of these steps is predictive models that generate predictions for the target variable. You can see the importance of this step in data mining and why it is crucial to get it right. Any mistakes made during this stage will result in invalid predictive models. To complete the modeling step effectively, it is essential to understand the underlying foundations of the machine learning methods we select and ensure proper configurations.

We will begin the modeling phase with one of the most popular data mining algorithms: regression. This chapter covers two regression methods—linear regression and logistic regression. Both are widely used across various fields due to their standardized, straightforward analysis process and easily interpretable results. These methods allow us to derive a regression equation that reflects the relationship between predictors and the target variable. For example, regression can be used to predict a customer's likelihood of purchasing a product or the risk of flight delays.

Linear regression is primarily an association method used when the target variable is continuous, with a linear relationship between the target variable and the predictors. In contrast, logistic regression is a classification method used when the target variable is binary (logistic regression) or categorical (multinomial logistic regression). This type of regression reflects a nonlinear relationship between predictors and the target variable, presented as a logit function.

211. Since regression methods are covered extensively in most statistics textbooks and courses, this chapter provides a brief overview of the statistical foundation, focusing more on how these methods are applied in data mining. I will use practical examples to demonstrate the data mining process and explain how to interpret the results. For those interested in diving deeper into the statistical foundations of these methods, I have included some recommended references for further reading.

What Is the Regression Method?

Regression is a widely used method that estimates the relationship between a dependent variable (target variable) and multiple independent variables (predictors). The goal of regression is to develop a mathematical function or model that can predict the values of the target variable based on the predictors. In many statistics books, the terms “dependent variable” and “independent variable” are commonly used. However, for consistency, I will use the terms “target variable” and “predictors” throughout this book. It's important to remember that the target variable is the same as the dependent variable and predictors are the same as independent variables.

Let's consider an example: Suppose we want to predict whether customers will choose to dine at a restaurant. Here, the target variable is the dining decision (Yes or No), while predictors may include factors such as gender, race, age, education, income, diet preference, and health condition. The regression model built from this data identifies predictors that significantly influence the dining decision and estimates mathematical relationships between those predictors and the target variable. More specifically, the regression method calculates the coefficients (weights) of the predictors in the model to minimize the difference between predicted values and the actual values of the target variable.

The primary advantage of regression is its simplicity in terms of understanding, usage, and interpretation. Since its mathematical foundation is similar to what is taught in most statistics courses, there is an abundance of resources that explain the algorithm in detail. In fact, most statistics or quantitative analysis books provide comprehensive explanations of this method and how the regression equation is estimated. In this book, I will focus more on the practical application and purpose of regression rather than delving into the detailed mathematical foundations. However, I will explain key terminologies and important aspects of the data analysis process as needed.

Linear Regression and Logistic Regression

There are two primary types of regression: linear regression and logistic regression. While both are regression methods, they have fundamental differences. Linear regression is used when the target variable is continuous, making it an association model. In some cases, a target variable measured using a Likert scale can be analyzed with linear regression, provided the intervals between levels are equal. As covered in Chapter 3, in such cases, Likert scale variables can be treated as interval variables.

On the other hand, logistic regression is used when the target variable is categorical (binary or nominal), making it a classification model. Binary variables have two levels, whereas nominal variables have more than two levels (multi-class). When the target variable is nominal, the model is often referred to as multinomial logistic regression. However, in data mining, the distinction between binary and nominal target variables is less of a concern as the focus shifts to model performance. To keep things simple, I will use the term “logistic regression” for both 212. binary and nominal target variables, specifying the scale of the target variable for clarification when necessary. Table 7.1 presents examples of both linear and logistic regressions, helping to illustrate the practical differences between these two methods.

TABLE 7.1 Examples of Linear Regression and Logistic Regression Return to text.⏎

Regression Methods

Examples

Linear regression example

The target variable is the students’ SAT scores, which is continuous, ranging from 0 to 1,600.

Predictors include age, gender, race, high school GPA, and family income.

Logistic regression example

The target variable is a student's decision to select a particular major, such as marketing. This is a binary variable (Yes or No).

Another example involves the student's choice of one of four majors: marketing, accounting, finance, or management. In this case, the target variable is nominal with four levels: 1 (marketing), 2 (accounting), 3 (finance), or 4 (management). Predictors include age, gender, race, high school GPA, and family income.

Due to differences in the target variable, linear and logistic regressions employ different estimation methods, resulting in variations in their assumptions, outputs, and the interpretation of results. Specifically, linear regression uses the ordinary least squares (OLS) method to estimate the regression equation while logistic regression relies on the maximum likelihood (ML) method for estimation.

The regression equations for these methods are shown below. To make the equations easier to understand, I’ve avoided typical mathematical notations and instead named the variables and coefficients in a more straightforward manner rather than using Greek characters.

For linear regression:


target = int + coe1 x predictor1 + coe2 x predictor2 + coe3 x predictor3 + … + error

For logistic regression:


logit(target) = int + coe1 x predictor1 + coe2 x predictor2 + coe3 x predictor3 + … + error

where

  • target is the target variable,

  • predictor is the predictor variable,

  • int is the intercept,

  • coe is the regression coefficient for the corresponding predictor,

  • error is the error terms.

You may notice that in logistic regression, we do not directly estimate the target variable but rather the logit value of that variable. Naturally, the concept of a logit value can be difficult to grasp. 213. Therefore, when interpreting logistic regression results, we use odds ratios rather than correlation coefficients. I will explain this in the section “How to Read and Understand Logistic Regression Results” later in this chapter.

The charts in Figure 7.1 illustrate how the linear regression equation differs from the logistic regression equation. As you can see, linear regression detects only the linear relationship between the target variable (Y) and the predictors (X). In contrast, logistic regression captures a nonlinear relationship between the target variable (Y) and the predictors (X) through the logit function. Since the target variable in logistic regression is binary (0 or 1), Y can only take on those two values. However, note that the relationship between logit(Y) and X remains linear, as shown in the equation.

Thus, while logistic regression can detect nonlinear relationships via the logit function, its ability to model nonlinearity is limited to this transformation and the linear effect of the correlation coefficients. This is a key difference between logistic regression and other nonlinear methods, such as decision trees, neural networks, or random forests, which can identify more complex forms of nonlinearity.

Table 7.2 highlights some key differences between linear regression and logistic regression. In the following sections, we will explore the details of both methods and how to configure models using these approaches.

TABLE 7.2 Differences between Linear Regression and Logistic Regression Return to text.⏎

Items

Linear Regression

Logistic Regression

Nature of the dependent variable

The target variable in linear regression is continuous and numeric, representing a range of real numbers. The model aims to establish a linear relationship between the predictors and the continuous outcome.

The target variable in logistic regression is binary or categorical, representing two or more discrete outcomes. The model predicts the probability of an event in one category.

Output and range

The output of linear regression is a continuous value, and the predicted values can be any real number. The range of predictions is not constrained.

The output of logistic regression is a probability score between 0 and 1, representing the likelihood of the event occurring.

Model function

The model function in linear regression is a linear equation that represents the weighted sum of the predictors plus an intercept term. The relationship between the variables is assumed to be linear.

The model function in logistic regression is the logistic (sigmoid) function, which represents the weighted sum of the predictors to a probability score. It models the odds of an event occurring. Note that the relationship between the odds of an event and predictors is assumed to be linear.

Applications

Linear regression is used for predicting and modeling continuous outcomes, such as predicting house prices, temperature, or sales volume based on various factors.

Logistic regression is used for binary or multinomial classification tasks, such as predicting whether an email is spam or not or classifying images into multiple categories.

Evaluation metrics

Linear regression uses common model fit metrics for association models plus F-test and R-squared (coefficient of determination).

Logistic regression uses common model fit metrics for classification models.

Optimization method

The model parameters in linear regression are typically estimated using methods like ordinary least squares (OLS) to minimize the sum of squares errors.

The model parameters in logistic regression are typically estimated using maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) to maximize the likelihood of the observed outcomes.
214.

Advantages and Disadvantages

It's important to note that in data mining, no machine learning method is perfect, regardless of its complexity. Every method comes with its own advantages and disadvantages. Therefore, it is crucial to understand these strengths and limitations in order to select the appropriate method and accurately interpret the results. Regression methods, for example, are grounded in statistical foundations, making them relatively easy to implement and understand. However, their linear nature and underlying assumptions can limit their effectiveness in predictive modeling. Table 7.3 summarizes the key advantages and disadvantages of these regression methods.

TABLE 7.3 Advantages and Disadvantages of Regression Methods Return to text.⏎

Regression Methods

Advantages

Disadvantages

Linear regression

  • Simple to implement.

  • Best for detecting linear patterns.

  • Outputs are easy to understand and interpret (regression coefficients, direction, p-value).

  • Works well with a small number of predictors.

  • Requires less data to work.

  • Less prone to overfitting.

  • Short computing time.

  • Subject to normality assumption.

  • Requires the linearity between the target variable and predictors.

  • Requires continuous variables.

  • Sensitive to missing values and outliers.

  • Unable to detect nonlinear relationships.

  • May not produce a good model fit with a large number of predictors.

  • Prone to multicollinearity, which limits us from analyzing big data.

Logistic regression

  • Simple to implement and efficient to train.

  • Provides regression coefficients, direction, and p-value for interpretation.

  • Provides probabilistic outputs.

  • Does not require normal distribution.

  • Works with both continuous and categorical predictors.

  • Can be extended to multiple classes (multinomial regression).

  • Able to detect nonlinearity through the logit function.

  • Less susceptible to overfitting.

  • Short computing time.

  • Requires a categorical target variable.

  • Assumes linearity between the logit value of the target variable and predictors.

  • Unable to detect all forms of nonlinear relationships.

  • Unable to detect complex patterns.

  • Prone to multicollinearity, which limits us from analyzing big data.

  • Probabilistic outputs are harder to understand and interpret.

  • Lack of interpretability for a nominal target variable with multi levels.

  • Requires more data for a good model fit.

Linear Regression

215.

Linear Regression Equation

Let's begin with a linear regression equation to understand the components of this method. As previously mentioned, the regression equation represents the mathematical relationships between the target variable and predictors. Linear regression is applicable only when the target variable is continuous. Here, we will present the linear regression equation in its traditional form, which helps you interpret outputs provided by various software applications. You can always refer to the simplified version shown earlier.


Y = β0 + β1x1 + β2x2 + … + βnxn + ε

Where

  • Y is the target variable,

  • x1 to xn are predictor variables (1 – n),

  • β0 is the intercept,

  • β1 – βn are the regression coefficients for the corresponding predictors,

  • ε is the residual or error.

Estimation Approach

An estimation approach refers to the statistical method used to calculate the values of all components in the regression equation, including the intercept, regression coefficients, and error terms. OLS is the standard estimation method for linear regression. It is commonly used to estimate the intercept and regression coefficients by minimizing the sum of squares errors (SSEs). The mathematical foundation of OLS is thoroughly explained in many statistics books, so I won’t elaborate here. What is important to emphasize is that using this method imposes strict assumptions on linear regression.

Assumption Requirements

216. In traditional statistical studies, linear regression is subject to strict assumptions to ensure the validity of the results. These include assumptions of normality, homoscedasticity, linearity, non-multicollinearity, continuous variables, and no missing values. If these assumptions are violated, the software can still run the analysis and produce outputs, but the validity of the results—and consequently the conclusions—becomes uncertain. In traditional settings, researchers typically work with a small number of predictors and a small sample size. For instance, with five predictors and an effect size of 0.25, a sample size of just 57 records is required. With ten predictors, the sample size increases only slightly to 75 records.

However, in data mining, we work with very large datasets containing many predictors and a large sample size. As a result, we have more flexibility in terms of meeting these assumptions when using linear regression. The Central Limit Theorem supports this flexibility, as it states that with a large enough sample size, the distribution of the sample can be assumed to be approximately normal. Therefore, when applying linear regression in data mining, we do not need to strictly meet all the assumptions, as is required in traditional studies.

That said, it is still advisable to address key assumptions to improve the performance of the regression model. For instance, handling and imputing missing values is highly recommended, as linear regression performs better with a complete dataset. Normalizing the data can also improve model fit by addressing the normality assumption. Additionally, managing outliers helps reduce noise in the data, leading to a more accurate model fit.

You may ask: Should we be concerned about the validity of the results if we do not meet the test assumptions? It's a good question, as we should always consider the reliability and validity of the results. In data mining studies, we implement additional rigorous steps to ensure the quality of the results. As mentioned in Chapter 3, we typically split the dataset into training, test, and validation samples. The training sample is used to build the model while the test and validation samples ensure the model's performance beyond just the training data, helping prevent overfitting. By comparing the model's results across these three samples, we can assess the model's performance and ensure its reliability and validity. Thus, even if we do not meet all assumptions, these steps allow us to maintain the validity of our predictive models.

Here are a few key assumptions for linear regression, along with the level of flexibility we have in data mining projects:

  • The target variable must be continuous: This assumption is crucial for establishing an association model. However, a target variable on a Likert scale is acceptable as long as the gaps between levels are equal.

  • Predictors must be continuous: There is more flexibility with this assumption. Although continuous predictors are preferable for interpretability and model fit, categorical (binary or nominal) predictors can still be used. These variables can be converted into dummy variables, for example, coding an education level variable (1—high school, 2—bachelor, and 3—graduate) into three separate variables: high school, bachelor, and graduate (with two levels, 1 for “yes” and 0 for “no”). While traditional statistical software often requires manual dummy coding, many data mining tools automate this process. Nonetheless, interpreting regression coefficients for dummy variables requires extra caution, as they are not as straightforward as with continuous variables.

  • Normality: Normality is a common assumption for parametric statistical methods, particularly with the OLS method. In data mining, with larger datasets, fully satisfying the normality 217. assumption is not always necessary. However, skewed data can still negatively impact model performance. Therefore, reviewing histograms and transforming variables to normalize data are recommended. Additionally, outliers can skew data, so reviewing histograms and box plots to identify and remove extreme outliers is also beneficial. Achieving full normality is not essential, but moving closer to a normal distribution generally improves model fit.

  • Non-multicollinearity: Linear regression assumes that predictors are independent. In traditional studies, multi-collinearity—inter-correlation among predictors—must be addressed before running the regression analysis. However, research suggests that increasing the sample size can reduce the impact of multi-collinearity. In data mining projects, where large datasets are common, multi-collinearity is typically not a major concern.

  • No missing values: In traditional statistical studies, regression analysis requires a complete dataset, and missing values must be addressed through imputation or elimination. Some software may even produce an error if missing values are detected. In data mining, however, models can still run with missing values. If the percentage of missing data is small, model performance is generally not significantly affected. Still, if more than 15% of values are missing, imputation is recommended, as a complete dataset generally leads to a better-fitting model.

Linear Regression Model Fit Evaluation

In the OLS process, evaluating the model fit is essential. But what exactly is model fit? We discussed this in detail in Chapter 6. Essentially, we have a theoretical regression model, represented by the regression equation, and we also have data for the target variable and all predictors. Our goal is to see how well the data aligns with the theoretical model—this alignment is what we refer to as model fit.


Residuals = Actual data – Predicted data

In Chapter 6, I covered the general model fit metrics for association models, including RMSE, MAPRE, residual sum of squares error (RSE), explanatory power (EP), the actual vs. predicted chart, and the residuals vs. predicted chart. In this chapter, I will focus specifically on metrics used for linear regression. In particular, when using linear regression, we need to evaluate the F-test and R2. Table 7.4 explains these metrics and how to interpret them.

TABLE 7.4 Model Fit Metrics Specific to Linear Regression Return to text.⏎

Metrics

Description

F-test

The F-test evaluates the significance of the overall model. A significant F-test indicates that the regression model fits the data better than a model with no predictors. A significant F-test is expected for a well-fitting model.

R2 (coefficient of determination)

R² is a common metric for assessing model fit in linear regression. It represents the percentage of variance in the target variable explained by the predictors. There is no absolute cutoff for a good R², as it depends on the number of predictors, but a general rule of thumb is as follows:

  • R² > 0.7: Good model fit

  • R² between 0.5 and 0.7: Acceptable model fit

  • R² < 0.5: Poor model fit

Keep in mind that R2 tends to decrease as the number of predictors increases, which is often the case in data mining. A lower R2 can still be acceptable with many predictors.

Adjusted R2

Adjusted R2 is a modified version of R2 that accounts only for predictors that significantly impact the model's performance. It is generally recommended to use adjusted R2 for evaluation. You can apply the same thresholds as suggested for R2 above.

218. In linear regression, when reviewing materials on the F-test and R2, you may encounter specific terminologies, notations, and formulas. I have included these in Table 7.5 for quick reference. Below are the formulas for calculating sum of squares total (SST) and R2 using sum of squares regression (SSR) and SSE:

TABLE 7.5 Key Terminologies and Notations in Linear Regression Return to text.⏎

Terminologies

Notations

Descriptions

Target variable

y

Actual value of the target variable (dependent variable).

Predictor

x

Actual value of the predictor (independent variable).

Mean of target variable

$\overset{-}{y}$

Mean value of the target variable.

Predicted value

ŷ

Predicted value of the target variable estimated by the model.

Error

e

Error (residual) is the difference between the actual and predicted values of the target variable.

Sum of squares error

SSE

A measure of how far the data points are from the model's predicted values.

Sum of squares total

SST

A measure of how far the data points are from the mean of the target variable.

Sum of squares regression

SSR

A measure of how far the mean is from the model's predicted values.


SST = SSR + SSE


$$R^{2} = \frac{SST - SSE}{SST} = \frac{Explained~variance}{Total~variance}$$

As explained in Chapter 6, these formulas apply exclusively to linear regression and not to other methods. As you can see, in linear regression, R2 is essentially the same as the EP that we discussed in Chapter 6.

Model Selection Process

In the regression modeling process, model selection is a crucial step in training the model. It determines how predictors are entered into the regression analysis. While it may seem logical to enter all variables at once and let the analysis identify significant predictors, doing so increases computing time and complicates model fitting. Interestingly, there are multiple ways to decide how variables are included in the model, and choosing the right selection method can significantly improve model fit.

Regression literature identifies three primary variable selection methods in linear regression: backward, forward, and stepwise. I will explain these methods simply, accompanied by diagrams for better understanding. Afterward, I will show you the specific methods used in SPSS Modeler, as this is the software we use for our analysis.

One important point to note is that all three methods are forms of the stepwise method, an iterative variable selection process used in data mining to identify the most relevant subset of variables for a predictive model. To avoid confusion, I refer to them as forward stepwise, backward stepwise, and adaptive stepwise. Each method results in multiple models, with the final 219. one typically being the best. Below, I describe the steps for each method, along with corresponding diagrams (Figure 7.2, Figure 7.3, Figure 7.4).

  • Forward Stepwise (Figure 7.2)

    1. The process begins with a model without any predictors (null model).

    2. The most significant variables are added to the model, one after the other. Significant variables are the ones significantly associated with the target variable. Typically, the most significant predictor is the one with the smallest p-value or provides the highest increase in R2.

    3. The selection will stop when all variables under consideration are added or a pre-determined stopping rule is met.

  • Backward Stepwise (Figure 7.3)

    1. The process begins with a model that includes all predictors (full model).

    2. The least significant variables are removed from the model, one after the other.

    3. The selection will stop when no variables are left or a pre-determined stopping rule is met.

  • Adaptive Stepwise (Figure 7.4): This method is similar to forward stepwise but with one key difference: After adding an additional variable to the model, it can remove a variable currently in the model but no longer significant. In other words, it is adaptive. This adaptability allows the model to evolve dynamically, and for this reason, in some cases, adaptive stepwise is also known as bidirectional stepwise.

    1. The process begins with a model without any predictors (null model).

    2. The most significant variables are added to the model, one after the other.

    3. After each addition, any variables already in the model that are no longer significant will be removed.

    4. The selection will stop when all variables under consideration are added or a pre-determined stopping rule is met.220.

221. The important question is: Which stepwise method should we use? Table 7.6 outlines scenarios where each method is appropriate. As discussed earlier, adaptive stepwise seems to be the most capable of selecting predictors that best predict the target variable. Unlike forward and backward stepwise methods, which follow a linear and sequential process, adaptive stepwise allows for the dynamic addition and removal of variables, resulting in the best model fit. In other words, it can select the best combination of predictors for model-fitting purposes. For this reason, adaptive stepwise is generally recommended for data mining. However, it has a few disadvantages, such as requiring more computing time and, in some cases, leading to overfitting. To mitigate this, cross-validation with sub-samples can be used to evaluate predictive power and avoid overfitting.

TABLE 7.6 When to Use Which Stepwise Method? Return to text.⏎

When to Use Forward Stepwise?

When to Use Backward Stepwise?

When to Use Adaptive Stepwise?

Large number of predictors

When dealing with a large number of potential predictors, forward stepwise is computationally more efficient, as it starts with an empty model and incrementally adds variables.

Multicollinearity concerns

If there are concerns about multicollinearity (high correlation) between predictors, backward stepwise helps identify and remove redundant predictors.

Exhaustive search

Adaptive stepwise allows for an exhaustive search of significant predictors without becoming overly computationally intensive.

Exploratory analysis

Forward stepwise is a good starting point for exploratory analysis, as it allows us to gradually build a model by adding variables that have a significant impact on the target variable.

Well-founded theoretical basis

When there is a strong theoretical basis or domain knowledge for what predictors are more important than others, backward stepwise is useful in eliminating less significant variables from the model.

Data exploration and model building

Adaptive stepwise is useful at the initial stages of data exploration and model building as it allows for a comprehensive examination of various predictor subsets and their impact on the model.

No prior knowledge

When there is no strong prior knowledge or theory about which predictors are likely to be relevant, forward stepwise helps identify potentially important predictors.

Complex models

Backward stepwise is particularly useful in complex models, where removing less relevant variables can improve the model's interpretability and generalization.

Model fit improvement

Since adaptive stepwise considers all possible combinations of predictors, it provides more robust results and improves the model fit.

Variable interaction analysis

When interactions between predictors are essential, adaptive stepwise helps identify relevant interaction terms that might not be captured by individual forward or backward selection.

Since SPSS Modeler uses different terminology for these methods, I have included a comparison in Table 7.7 to avoid confusion. Note that SPSS Modeler provides distinct estimation methods for both linear and logistic regressions. In this book, I refer to the three methods discussed above for both algorithms to ensure consistency.

TABLE 7.7 SPSS Modeler's Terms and Equivalent Terms Return to text.⏎

Backwards

Stepwise

How to Read and Understand the Regression Equation and Results?

222. After running a regression analysis, the first step is to evaluate the model fit using the recommended metrics, such as R2, F-test, RMSE, MAPE, RSE, EP, the actual vs. predicted chart, and the residuals vs. predicted chart. If all criteria are met and indicate a good model fit, the next step is to report and interpret the regression outputs. But how do we make sense of those outputs, and what conclusions can we draw?

These are common questions when conducting any data analysis, and they are even more crucial in data mining, where models often include a large number of predictors. To simplify the interpretation process, let's first review some simple hypothetical regression equations. For ease of understanding, I will limit the number of predictors. Later in this chapter, we will look at actual regression results using SPSS Modeler in a data mining example.

For linear regression, the estimation results typically include the following information:

  • Intercept

  • Unstandardized regression coefficient (B)

  • Standard error for B

  • Standardized regression coefficients (beta)

  • t-value

  • Probability value (p-value)

  • 95% confidence interval for B

To interpret the regression results correctly, we focus on the probability value (p-value), unstandardized coefficients, and standardized coefficients. Table 7.8 explains these terms and how to use them when interpreting regression results.

TABLE 7.8 Probability Value, Unstandardized Regression Coefficient, and Standardized Regression Coefficient Return to text.⏎

Terms

Description

Probability value (p-value)

The probability value (p-value) is a statistical measure for assessing the significance of the estimated coefficients (also known as the regression weights or beta values) for the predictors in the regression model. It determines whether the relationship between each predictor and the target variable is statistically significant or if it could have occurred by chance.

Significance level (alpha)

The significance level (alpha) is the threshold used in hypothesis testing to determine statistical significance. It represents the maximum probability of rejecting the null hypothesis when it is actually true (commonly set at 0.05).

Unstandardized regression coefficient (B)

The unstandardized regression coefficient (B) quantifies the relationship between a predictor and the target variable in its original units of measurement. It shows the expected change in the target variable for a one-unit change in the predictor, holding all other variables constant.

Standardized regression coefficient (beta)

The standardized regression coefficient (beta) quantifies the relationship between a predictor and the target variable after both are standardized to a common scale (typically in terms of standard deviations). Standardized coefficients range between 0 and 1 and make comparisons between predictors easier since they are on the same scale.

Probability Value (p-Value)

The p-value is a statistical measure used to assess the significance of the estimated coefficients (also known as regression weights or beta values) of the predictors in a regression model. It indicates whether the relationship between each predictor and the target variable is statistically significant or if it could have occurred by chance. The threshold for determining statistical significance is called the significance level (alpha), with the most commonly used significance level being 0.05 (5%).

223. If the p-value is less than or equal to the significance level (p ≤ α), it suggests that the coefficient is statistically significant. For example, in a linear regression model where the target variable is students’ SAT scores, suppose the analysis reveals that GPA and family income have p-values lower than 0.05. This would indicate that these two predictors are statistically significant and have a meaningful impact on predicting SAT scores.

Unstandardized Regression Coefficients (B)

After identifying significant predictors, the next step is to explain their relationships with the target variable using unstandardized regression coefficients (B). Unstandardized coefficients quantify the relationship between each predictor and the target variable in their original units of measurement.

In our example of predicting SAT scores, suppose the regression results show unstandardized coefficients of 120 for GPA and 0.01 for family income, with an intercept of 105. The regression equation would be as follows:


SAT score = 105 + 120 × GPA + 0.01 × Family income

This equation includes the intercept and unstandardized coefficients. It suggests that GPA and family income are significant predictors of SAT scores, both positively correlated with the SAT score. These predictors represent the student's academic performance (via GPA) and the family's financial resources for education and SAT tutoring (via income).

Using this equation, we can predict a student's SAT score based on known values of these predictors. More importantly, we can interpret how changes in each predictor affect the target variable. For example, with a coefficient of 120 for GPA, a one-point increase in GPA results in a 120-point increase in the SAT score. Similarly, an increase in family income by $1 results in a 0.01-point increase in SAT scores. In practical terms, an increase of $10,000 in family income would raise the SAT score by 100 points (0.01 × 10,000 = 100).

224. Note that the error term is not included in this equation because we have already used it to evaluate model fit. The error represents the difference between predicted and actual SAT scores, and since our model fit is good, the error is considered acceptable. At this stage, the focus is on using the equation to predict changes in SAT scores based on the changes in significant predictors, making the error term less relevant for interpretation.

Standardized Regression Coefficients (Beta)

One thing to notice about unstandardized coefficients is that they depend on the unit of measurement of the predictor, making them scale-dependent. For example, while GPA may have a higher regression coefficient than family income, we can’t directly compare their impact because GPA is measured in points and income in USD. To make meaningful comparisons, we use standardized coefficients.

A standardized regression coefficient measures the relationship between a predictor and the target variable after both have been standardized to a common scale. Standardized coefficients range from 0 to 1 and are expressed in terms of standard deviations, making them scale-independent and directly comparable across predictors.

For instance, if the standardized coefficients for GPA and family income are 0.68 and 0.34, respectively, we can conclude that GPA has twice the effect size of family income in predicting SAT scores. In this case, GPA is more important than family income by a factor of two.

To identify and rank important predictors, it is recommended to use standardized coefficients and rank them from highest to lowest. In data mining, a more generic term used to capture the significance of predictors is “relative importance.”

Example: Linear Regression

In this example, we conduct a linear regression analysis using the Boston dataset in SPSS Modeler. In the Chapter 3 exercise, you had the opportunity to explore the data. Now, in this chapter, we will build a predictive model using linear regression.

  • Dataset: Boston.sav

  • Target variable: Imv (Continuous—Median home value)

The Boston Housing dataset contains housing data from the Boston, MA, area collected by the U.S. Census Bureau. The dataset includes 14 fields, as outlined in Table 7.9. All fields are continuous (the Charles_River field, originally binary, has been dummy-coded into a continuous variable). The target field is Imv, representing the median home values in the area.

225. We have completed three important steps in the data mining process for the Boston dataset: Data Exploration, Transformation, and Sampling. Since these steps were thoroughly covered in Chapters 3, 4, and 5, I won’t repeat the procedures or results here. However, I will summarize these tasks and present them in the stream for easier reference.

Data Exploration

In this step, the Data Audit 1 node is used to generate histograms for all continuous fields and produces descriptive statistics. The data exploration results show that the dataset contains 506 records. The target field (Imv) has 54 missing values, but the predictors do not have any missing values. Since linear regression performs better with a complete dataset, it is necessary to impute those missing values.

Additionally, most fields do not follow normal distributions based on their skewness and kurtosis values (these values should ideally be between −0.5 and 0.5 for data to be considered normally distributed). The histograms reveal that some fields, including Imv, Age, and Tax, are slightly skewed, with a few outliers. Other fields exhibit significant skewness and will require normalization (for more details, refer to the Boston dataset example in Chapter 3).

226.

Data Sampling

Typically, the next step is sampling. The dataset contains 506 records, and since this is relatively small, we will use all the records for analysis. Therefore, no data sampling is performed at this stage. The primary task in this step is data partitioning, but we will address that after data modification.

Data Modification

As mentioned earlier, most input fields exhibit non-normal distributions, and the target field (Imv) contains missing values. In this step, we perform data imputation and normalization.

  • Data imputation: Using the Quality tab from the Data Audit 1 output, we generate a SuperNode labeled “Missing Value Imputation,” which replaces missing values in the Imv field with the mean value.

  • Data normalization: To normalize the data, we apply the Transform node to select appropriate transformation functions. This generates a SuperNode called “Supernode_Transform,” which normalizes most input fields except for Imv, Age, and Tax, as they already exhibit near-normal distributions (see the Boston example in Chapter 5 for more details).

Data Partition

Before building the regression model, it is essential to partition the data. Since the sample size is smaller than 1,000, as recommended in Chapter 4, we partition the data into training and test samples using a 60-40 split ratio. No validation sample is created in this case. The Partition node follows the Super_Transform node in the workflow.

You can set up a data partition using the following selection. This process divides the data into two sub-samples: The training sample (60% of the data) will be used to train the model while the test sample (40% of the data) will be used to evaluate the model's performance.

227.

Modeling

Our goal is to build and execute a linear regression model for the target field Imv. There are several methods available for model creation, and SPSS Modeler offers a variety of tools in the Modeling group. To explore which method offers the best predictive power, I will build four different linear regression models and compare them. The specifics of these models are outlined in Table 7.10.

TABLE 7.10 Descriptions and Configurations of the Regression Models Return to text.⏎

Linear Regression Models

Configurations

  • Mean imputation method for the field Imv.

  • Specific transformation functions (as indicated in Chapter 5) used to normalize 11 continuous fields (excluding Imv, Age, and Tax). Transformed input fields are used to train the model.

  • Regression model: the Stepwise method

Regression 1 node (under Modeling group), following the Missing Value Imputation, Supernode_Transform, and Partition nodes.

With these four regression models, we will have a comprehensive stream that includes all steps of the data mining process. The stream will display how to build these regression models, the flow of nodes, and the connections between steps. I will also provide specific instructions for setting up the configurations for each model.

228. How to Set Up the Regression 1 Model

  1. Open SPSS Modeler.

  2. Create a new stream and name it “Boston_Regression.”

  3. Add the data source Boston.sav to the stream.

  4. Add a Type node to the stream and connect it to the data source. Open the Type node settings.

  5. Double-check field names, measurements, and roles.

  6. Set the role for the field Imv as Target. All other fields should be set as Input.

  7. 229. Perform imputation and transformation using SuperNodes as described above. After completing these steps, you should have the SuperNode Missing Value Imputation for imputation and the SuperNode Supernode_Transform for normalization.

  8. Add another Type node to the stream and connect it to the SuperNode Supernode_Transform. Open the Type node settings.

  9. Since the transformed data is used for most fields (except for Imv, Age, and Tax) to train the regression model, set the role of unused fields as None. This step ensures SPSS Modeler does not use those fields in the next analysis. The predefined Target and Input fields will be passed on to the next node for analysis.

  10. Click Apply, and then click OK.

  11. 230. Add a Partition node to the stream and connect it to this Type node. Open the Partition node settings.

  12. Select Train and test and set the training partition size to 60 and the testing partition size to 40 (refer to the Data Partition step above for details).

  13. Click Apply, and then click OK.

  14. From the Modeling group, add a Regression node to the stream, name it Regression 1, and connect it to the Partition node. Open the Regression node settings.

  15. Under the Model tab, select Use partition data, Build model for each split, and Include constant in equation.

  16. Select Stepwise for the Method.

  17. Under the Analyze tab, select Calculate predictor importance.

  18. Click Apply and Run.

  19. SPSS Modeler will run and add the model nugget (result node) to the stream. If there are errors while running the model, the software will display an error message.

  20. 231. From the Output group, add an Analysis node to the stream and connect it to the model nugget Regression 1. This node will compare the model performance between the training and test samples. Open the Analysis node settings.

  21. Under the Analysis tab, select Performance evaluation, Evaluation metric, Confidence figures, and Separate by partition.

  22. Click Apply and Run.

Extracting Model Fit Results

The Analysis node results show the model's performance for both the training and test samples. In this output, the field $E-Imv represents the predicted value of the target field while Imv is the actual (observed) value of the target field. Most of the metrics are straightforward. Remember, error refers to the difference between observed and predicted values.

Below is a brief description of the key metrics:

  • Minimum error: The smallest error value.

  • Maximum error: The largest error value.

  • Mean error: The average of errors across all records, indicating any potential systematic bias in the model.

  • Mean absolute error (MAE): The average of the absolute errors across all records, showing the average magnitude of error.

  • 232. Standard deviation: The standard deviation of the errors.

  • Linear correlation: The linear correlation between the predicted and actual values, ranging from −1 to 1.

  • Occurrences: The sample size. In this case, 304 records are used for training the model and 202 records are used for testing the model.

As discussed in Chapter 6, these metrics alone are not ideal for evaluating model performance and comparison. Specifically, for association models, it is recommended to use metrics like RMSE, MAPE, RSE, and EP. Additionally, metrics specific to linear regression—including F-test, R2, and adjusted R2—should be used. However, since SPSS Modeler does not provide RMSE, MAPE, RSE, and EP directly through the Analysis node output, we will need to export the prediction outputs to Excel and calculate these metrics separately (see the section “Steps to Export Regression 1 Output to Excel” later in this chapter.).

One important thing to note is that regression-specific metrics, such as the F-test, R2, and adjusted R2, are only provided for the training sample. While these can be used for a preliminary evaluation of the regression model, they are not suitable for model comparison and reliability evaluation.

Extracting F-test, R2, and Adjusted R2

To extract the F-test, R2, and adjusted R2 from SPSS Modeler, these values are stored in the model nugget rather than in the Analysis node. You can access the model nugget to view these regression-specific metrics.

Follow the steps below to extract F-test, R2, and adjusted R2 for our Regression 1 model. Note that these results are based on the training sample, which we can use for model comparison.

  1. Double-click the model nugget Regression 1 from the stream. The Regression 1 result window will open.

  2. Under the Advanced tab, select Regression/Model Summary. You will see that the algorithm ran nine models during the stepwise process to find the final model. Model 9 is the final model with R2 = 0.735 and adjusted R2 = 0.727.

  3. Select the ANOVA tab, where you can view the F-test for Model 9, which is 90.629.

As explained earlier, in linear regression, R2 is equivalent to EP, and RSE can be calculated as 1 − EP. Therefore, we have EP = R2 = 0.735 and RSE = 1 − EP = 1 − 0.735 = 0.265. In other words, based on the training sample results, this model has an EP of 73.5%, meaning it can explain 73.5% of the variance in the target field (Imv) based on the variance in the predictors.

That's how you extract these metrics. I will dive deeper into the details of the regression model once we identify the champion model.

Regression Models 2, 3, and 4 Setup

233. Follow the same steps as outlined for Regression 1 to set up and configure Regression Models 2, 3, and 4, using the configurations and nodes described in Table 7.10. Specifically:

Regression 2:

  • Use imputed data without normalization.

  • Use the Regression node with the Stepwise method.

Regression 3:

  • Use the Auto Data Prep node with the objective set to Balance speed and accuracy (no outlier handling).

  • Use the Regression node with the Stepwise method.

Regression 4:

  • Use the Auto Data Prep node with the objective set to Optimize for accuracy (with outlier handling).

  • Use the Regression node with the Stepwise method.

Running the Models

Run each model separately and add the Analysis node, as described for Regression 1. Once the models are run, follow the same steps to extract the model fit metrics from the Analysis node for the testing sample.

The next step is to evaluate the validity of the champion model by using complete model fit metrics. 235. Steps to Export Regression 1 Output to Excel:

  1. Add a Type node to the stream and connect it to the model nugget for Regression 1. Open the node settings.

  5. Click Apply and Run.

To further examine the model fit, we refer to the charts created in MS Excel using the data exported from the Export node. We focus on the testing results, as described in Chapter 6, because the testing sample is used to validate the model.

  • The actual vs. predicted chart (Figure 7.5) shows that most data points are scattered around the diagonal line, though there are some outliers.

In summary, the model's predictive power is considered acceptable, though not exceptional. In the following chapters, we will explore other methods to build additional predictive models.

Creating the Actual by Predicted Chart in SPSS Modeler

In addition to using Excel, you can create these charts directly in SPSS Modeler by using a scatter plot, as discussed in Chapter 3. Follow the steps below to create the Actual by Predicted chart:

  1. Continue with the Regression 1 stream from above.237.

  2. 238. From the Graphs group, add a Graphboard node to the stream and connect it to the Type node. Open the Graphboard settings.

  3. Under the Basic tab, select the fields Imv and $E-Imv on the left, and then choose Scatter plot on the right.

  4. Under the Detailed tab, set $E-Imv for X and Imv for Y.

  5. Click Apply and Run.

239. You will generate a scatter plot that shows the Actual by Predicted chart (Figure 7.7). This chart will look the same as the one you created earlier using Excel (Figure 7.5).

Creating the Residual by Predicted Chart in SPSS Modeler

To create the Residual by Predicted chart in SPSS Modeler, an extra step is required to calculate the residuals using the Derive node. After that, you can use the Graphboard to generate a scatter plot for the residuals against the predicted values ($E-Imv).

Follow the steps as given below:

  1. Continue with the Regression 1 stream.

  2. From the Field Ops group, add a Derive node to the stream and connect it to the Type node. Open the Derive settings.

  3. 240. For Derive field, enter Residual.

  4. For Formula, enter the following formula: Imv - $E-Imv. This will calculate the residual values and add them to the dataset in the Residual field.

  5. Click Apply and OK.

  6. From the Graphs group, add a Graphboard node to the stream and connect it to the Type node. Open the Graphboard settings.

  7. Under the Basic tab, select the fields Residual and $E-Imv on the left, and then choose Scatter plot on the right.

  8. Under the Detailed tab, set $E-Imv for X and Residual for Y.

  9. Click Apply and Run.

You will now generate a scatter plot displaying the residual by predicted ($E-Imv) values (Figure 7.8). This chart will be identical to the residual by predicted chart you previously created in Excel (Figure 7.6).

I’ve shown you both methods for creating these charts, and you can choose whichever you’re more comfortable with. While using Excel may be quicker and easier if you’re familiar with it, 241. knowing how to create these charts in SPSS Modeler is a valuable skill, as it can be applied to many similar tasks.

Regression Equation Interpretation

We have established that Regression 1 is the champion model, and its overall reliability and validity are acceptable. The next step is to interpret the model structure and regression equation to explain the effects of the significant predictors. For this, we use the regression output from SPSS Modeler. Interpretation of Key Predictors

  • Tax: This is a non-transformed variable. For every one-point increase in the full-value property tax rate per $10,000, the median house value decreases by $12 (0.012 × 1,000).

  • LogDistance_t: If the logarithm of the weighted distance to Boston employment centers increases by one point, the median house value decreases by $8,383 (8.383 × 1,000).

  • Lstat_t: If the square root of the percent lower-status population increases by one point, the median house value decreases by $3,583.

  • RmSQ_t: If the inverse of the average number of rooms per dwelling increases by one room, the median house value increases by $221,525.

  • 243. ZonePR_t: If the square root of the proportion of residential land zoned for large lots increases by one point, the median house value increases by $305.

  • CrimePC_t: If the square root of the crime rate per capita increases by one point, the median house value increases by $1,554.

Conclusion on Data Transformation

While transforming fields to normalize the data can improve model fit, it also introduces challenges in interpreting the results. Therefore, data transformation should only be performed when necessary. If a model with transformed data performs similarly to one without transformation, it is often preferable to use the non-transformed data for ease of interpretation.

Comparing the Effects of Predictors on Imv

To compare the effects of the predictors on the target field Imv, we should use standardized regression coefficients (also known as beta coefficients). These values, presented in Table 7.14, allow for a direct comparison of the relative impact of each predictor, regardless of the units of measurement.

However, SPSS Modeler offers a more intuitive method for comparing predictor importance through the variable importance chart (Figure 7.9). This chart visually ranks the predictors based on their importance in the model.

The chart shows that RmSQ is the most important predictor, followed by Tax, Lstat, Charles_River, and ZonePR. On the other hand, CrimePC and LogDistance are the least important predictors in the model.

What is the Linear Node in SPSS Modeler?

In addition to the Regression node, which is commonly used for performing linear regression in a traditional way, SPSS Modeler offers another node called Linear. The Linear node is an automatic linear modeling tool that handles all the steps in the linear regression process automatically. This includes data preparation, transformation, model selection, ensemble construction, and result presentation. Essentially, once the measurement scales and roles for the fields in the 244. data are defined, the Linear node takes over the entire data mining process. However, since most decisions are made automatically by the software, the researcher has limited control and customization options.

For demonstration purposes, I will use the Linear node to run a linear regression analysis on the Boston housing dataset and compare the results with the four previously created regression models.

Description and Configuration of Regression 5

  • Description: Automatic linear modeling (data preparation and model configuration are handled automatically by the software).

  • Configurations:

    • Objective: Create a standard model (we are not constructing ensembles here, as this topic will be covered later in Chapter 10).

    • Basis: Automatically prepare the data, including adjustment of measurement levels, handling of outliers, and treatment of missing values.

    • Model selection: Forward stepwise.

    • Criteria for entry/removal: Information criterion (AICC).

Steps to Add and Set Up the Linear Node

  1. Continue with the stream that contains the four previous regression models.

  2. From the Modeling group, add a Linear node to the stream and connect it to the Type node (the one following the data source). Name it Regression 5. Open the Linear node settings.

  3. Accept all the default settings of the node. Verify that the configurations are as follows:

    • Objective: Create a standard model.

    • Basis: Automatically prepare the data.

    • Model selection: Forward stepwise.

    • Criteria for entry/removal: Information criterion (AICC).

  4. Click Apply and then Run the node.

  5. Once the run is complete, a model nugget labeled Regression 5 will be added to the stream.

  6. 245. Add an Analysis node to the stream and connect it to the model nugget Regression 5. Open the Analysis node settings.

  7. Under the Analysis tab, select the following options: Performance evaluation, Evaluation metric, Confidence figures, and Separate by partition.

  8. Click Apply and then Run.

As you can see, the process is simple, easy, quick, and seamless, requiring no prior understanding of the regression algorithm. The output from the Analysis node provides metrics such as the MAE, mean error, standard error, and correlation (as described earlier). To access additional metrics, you need to open the model nugget.

You’ll notice that this output differs significantly from the Regression node's output. First, you still receive some overall results, including the adjusted R2 and the predictor importance chart. Additionally, the output automatically generates the predicted vs. observed chart (similar to the actual vs. predicted chart) without requiring any extra steps.

However, unlike the Regression node, this output does not include an Advanced tab, which would normally provide the model summary, analysis of variance (ANOVA), and coefficients. As a result, we don’t have access to metrics such as the R2 and the F-test. To compensate, I added the MAE and used the adjusted R2 as the EP to compare this model with the four other models we created earlier (refer to Table 7.16).

To further evaluate the model fit, we will examine the predicted by observed chart (Figure 7.10). The data points appear scattered around the diagonal line, indicating a good model fit. Unfortunately, the Linear node does not provide detailed regression outputs, such as the model summary, ANOVA, or coefficients. As a result, we cannot observe the number of steps in the stepwise process nor the changes in R2, F-tests, or coefficients for significant predictors. Keep in mind that the Linear node is designed to perform linear regression analysis quickly and automatically, which means it does not guarantee the production of a well-fitting model every time.

For these reasons, I recommend using the Regression node to gain more control and customization over the modeling process. The Regression node allows for adjustments to the model configuration, offering greater flexibility in achieving a good fit. However, the Linear node can be useful for running a preliminary regression analysis, providing quick insights into your model and data. Based on these initial results, you can make informed decisions regarding data modifications and modeling plans to improve your predictive model.246.

Logistic Regression

247.

Logistic Regression Equation

Logistic regression is used with a binary or nominal target variable. The traditional logistic regression equation is as follows:


$$Logit\left( Y \right) = log\left( \frac{p}{1 - p} \right) = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}x_{1} + \beta_{2}x_{2} + \ldots + \beta_{n}x_{n} + \varepsilon$$

where

  • Y is the target variable,

  • p is the probability of the event in the target variable,

  • x1 to xn are predictor variables 1 − n.

  • β0 is the intercept

  • β1 – βn are regression coefficients for the corresponding predictors,

  • ε is the residual or error.

Another form of this equation, which is easier to interpret, expresses the odds ratio as follows:


$$Odds\left( Y \right) = \left( \frac{p}{1 - p} \right) = e^{(\beta_{0} + \beta_{1}x_{1} + \beta_{2}x_{2} + \ldots + \beta_{n}x_{n} + \varepsilon)~}$$

Don’t be intimidated by these equations! We won’t use them directly in the analysis or interpretation of the results. I will explain the results in a simpler way.

Estimation Approach

Logistic regression estimates the target variable and regression coefficients differently from linear regression. The method used is maximum likelihood estimation (MLE). Simply put, we first assume a probability distribution for the target variable. Then, a likelihood function is used to calculate the probability of an outcome based on the predictors. This method is useful for estimating the probability of an event and does not require strict assumptions like OLS.

Assumption Requirements

As mentioned, due to the nature of the MLE method, logistic regression does not require strict assumptions like normality, homoscedasticity, or linearity. However, logistic regression typically involves the following assumptions:

  • Binary target variable: The target variable must be binary, meaning it has two distinct levels (e.g., 1—accident, 0—no accident).

  • Multiple predictors: Logistic regression requires multiple predictors but does not require them to be continuous. It works well with binary or nominal predictors, offering flexibility in scale. This is advantageous when analyzing large datasets with predictors on different scales.

  • Non-multicollinearity: Similar to linear regression, predictors must be independent of each other. However, with large sample sizes, the effect of multicollinearity is often tolerable.

  • Linearity: There must be a linear relationship between the predictors and the logit of the target variable. The equation shows a linear regression relationship between the logit of the target variable and the predictors.

In conclusion, logistic regression offers more flexibility in its assumptions, making it a robust method for data mining across various types of data.

Model Fit Evaluation

248. Logistic regression is a classification model, so we evaluate its performance using classification metrics, as described in Chapter 6. These include the following:

  • Misclassification rate

  • Accuracy rate

  • Sensitivity

  • Specificity

  • F1 score

  • Gini coefficient

  • Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve

  • Lift chart

Additionally, logistic regression has specific model fit metrics similar to those used in linear regression. Table 7.17 summarizes these metrics, allowing us to compare model fit between these regression methods.

The Chi-square test and pseudo R2 are specific metrics used to evaluate logistic regression models. To understand the Chi-square test for the −2 Log Likelihood (−2LL) difference, it's important to first grasp the concept of −2LL. For this reason, I have included a description of −2LL in Table 7.18.

TABLE 7.18 Recommended Method-Specific Metrics for Logistic Regression Return to text.⏎

Logistic Regression Metrics

Description

−2LL (−2 Log Likelihood)

A measure of how well the model fits the likelihood. A good model is characterized by a high likelihood of the observed results or a low −2LL. In the ideal scenario where a model perfectly fits the data, the likelihood attains a value of 1, and the −2LL score becomes 0.

Chi-square test of −2LL difference

(Omnibus test of model coefficients)

The difference in −2LL between two models in a stepwise process. A significant Chi-square test indicates improvement in the modeling step.

Pseudo R2

A measure of how well the model fits the data, compared to a model that always predicts the mean.

The two most common pseudo R2 are

  • McFadden's R2

  • Cox and Snell R2

Note that pseudo R2 does not range from 0 to 1 as it has a much lower upper bound. Hence, the general rule of thumb is that a pseudo R2 between 0.2 and 0.4 is considered a good fit.

Model Selection Methods

249. In logistic regression, we also have three stepwise methods, similar to those used in linear regression: forward stepwise, backward stepwise, and adaptive stepwise. Even though logistic regression deals with a binary target variable rather than a continuous one, it utilizes the same types of stepwise methods.

I recommend starting with the adaptive stepwise method for variable selection, as it allows us to find the best combination of predictors that leads to a well-fitting model.

How to Read and Understand Logistic Regression Results

Before interpreting logistic regression results, we must ensure we have a good model fit. Let's assume that we have already checked the logistic regression model fit metrics, such as −2LL, the Chi-square test for −2LL, pseudo R2, RMSE, RSE, EP, misclassification rate, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, F1 score, Gini coefficient, ROC chart, and Lift chart, and found the model fit to be satisfactory.

The next step is to interpret the logistic regression results to identify significant predictors and their effects on the target variable.

Typically, the logistic regression estimation results include the following:

  • Logistic coefficient (B)

  • Standard error

  • Wald statistic—a test for the significance of the coefficients

  • Degrees of freedom

  • Probability value (p-value)

  • Exp(B) or odds ratio

  • 95% confidence interval for Exp(B)

We focus on the key outputs that help us interpret the results. Logistic regression can be more challenging to read due to the use of the logit function. To simplify the process, we will primarily focus on the p-value, logistic coefficients, and odds ratio.

For example, suppose the regression equation for a model predicting students’ decision to choose major A is as follows:


Logit(majorA_choice) = 0.5 – 0.3 x gender + 0.4 + age

In this equation, 0.5 is the intercept, −0.3 is the logistic coefficient for gender, and 0.4 is the coefficient for age. The sign of the coefficient indicates the direction of the effect. In this case, gender has a negative effect on the choice of major A, while age has a positive effect.

While coefficients indicate the size of the effect, interpreting them in relation to the logit value (instead of the actual target variable) can be difficult. To make interpretation easier, we use the odds ratio. The equivalent equation in terms of odds is as follows:


Odds(majorA_choice) = e(0.5 –0.3 * gender  + 0.4 * age)

Most statistical software provides the odds ratio for each predictor alongside the coefficients. The sign of the coefficient indicates the direction of the effect, while the odds ratio helps us interpret the magnitude of the predictor's effect on the target variable.

For example, let's say we obtain the following odds ratios for gender and age:

  • Odds ratio for gender = 0.74

  • Odds ratio for age = 1.49

250. How do we interpret these numbers? First, let's consider gender, which in this case is a binary variable (e.g., Male and Female). Suppose Male is the reference category. This means switching from Male to Female reduces the odds of choosing major A by 26% (since 0.74 − 1 = −0.26). In other words, male students are 1/0.74 = 1.35 times more likely than female students to choose major A.

For age, the odds ratio of 1.49 means that for every one-year increase in age, the odds of a student choosing major A increase by 49% (since 1.49 − 1 = 0.49).

As you can see, interpreting logistic regression results can be more challenging than interpreting linear regression results. However, by following this process, we can effectively understand the results. We’ll explore this further with an actual example later.

We have completed three key steps in the data mining process in Chapters 3, 4, and 5: data exploration, data modification, and data sampling. I will not repeat the detailed steps here, as you can revisit those chapters to see the process in SPSS Modeler and the results. However, I will summarize the stream and primary findings from each step below so you can observe the connections between them and the decisions required to build a predictive model.

251.

Data Exploration

Data exploration was primarily conducted using the Data Audit 1 node, which generated graphs and descriptive statistics for the relevant fields. The exploration revealed a total of 124,464 records in the dataset. Three continuous fields were identified with missing values: arrival delay, departure delay, and flight time. Since the missing values accounted for less than 3% of the data, they will need to be imputed to prevent information loss.

Additionally, the price sensitivity field, which is based on a Likert scale, should have values ranging from 1 to 5. However, the presence of zero values indicates missing data that was not properly coded. By examining the histograms for the continuous fields, we found that most of them are not normally distributed. However, since the logistic regression algorithm does not require normality assumptions, normalization is not necessary.

Data Sampling

Typically, the next step is sampling. The dataset contains 124,464 records, and although it's possible to sample a subset for analysis, we will use the entire dataset since this sample size is not particularly large. Some advanced algorithms we’ll be using later, such as neural networks or random forests, often require a large dataset to train the model effectively. Therefore, no data sampling will be performed here. The main task in this step is data partitioning, which will be done after data modification.

Data Modification

As identified in the data exploration phase, there are three main issues with the data:

  1. Incorrect coding of missing values in the price sensitivity field.

  2. Missing values in three other fields: departure delay, arrival delay, and flight time.

  3. Non-normal distributions in most continuous fields.

Since we are using logistic regression, normalization is unnecessary. Therefore, the two primary data modification techniques we’ll use are replacement and imputation.

  • Replacement: We use the Filter node to recode the zero values in the price sensitivity field, which are incorrectly coded as missing values.

  • Imputation: Now, four fields have missing values: price sensitivity, departure delay, arrival delay, and flight time. To handle these missing values, we configure imputation methods using the Quality tab from the Data Audit 2 output. Specifically:

    • Mean imputation is applied to departure delay, arrival delay, and flight time.

    • Mid-range imputation is applied to price sensitivity (since it uses a Likert scale).

252. A SuperNode labeled Missing Value Imputation is generated to carry out the imputation. The results show the following number of missing values imputed:

  • Price sensitivity: 3,976 records

  • Departure delay: 2,201 records

  • Arrival delay: 2,565 records

  • Flight time: 2,565 records

Similar to the Boston Housing example, I added the Type node after each step, allowing us to check the field names, measurement scales, and roles. This helps ensure the fields are correctly defined for the next step. Additionally, I use the Data Audit node to view descriptive statistics and charts after each step, aiding in decision-making for subsequent steps.

Data Partition

In this step, we partition the data before building the logistic regression model. Since we have enough data, as recommended in Chapter 4, we partition the dataset into three sub-samples using a 60–20–20 split ratio:

  • Train (60%): Used to train the model.

  • Test (20%): Used to test the model.

  • Validation (20%): Used for final model assessment.

The Partition node is applied after the SuperNode Missing Value Imputation.

Refer to the screenshot below for setting up the data partition. It divides the dataset into the three sub-samples mentioned above. The training sample (60% of the data) is used to train the model, the test sample (20%) for testing the model, and the validation sample (20%) for final model evaluation.

253. As shown in Figures 7.12 and 7.13, the Partition node splits the data into three sub-samples based on the 60-20-20 ratio. The imbalance ratio between the levels for the two fields—airline recommendation and passenger class—remains consistent across the sub-samples. You can create additional charts for other fields as well. Therefore, we can conclude that the sub-samples are representative of the full dataset.

Modeling

254. Our objective is to build and run a logistic regression model with the target field being airline recommendation. Since this is a binary field, we will use binomial logistic regression rather than multinomial regression, which is used for target fields with multiple levels.

There are various approaches to building the model, using different data transformation options and SPSS Modeler tools. To explore the best approach, I will build four different logistic regression models and compare them to determine which one offers the best predictive power. Table 7.20 provides descriptions and configurations for each model.
