With these four regression models, we will create a comprehensive stream that shows the flow of nodes and the steps in the data mining process. I will provide instructions on setting up configurations for each model.

255. One important note: If we connect the Partition node directly to the Logistic node when running the analysis, SPSS Modeler will return an error message stating that the categorical input fields have incorrect values (due to string formats). Therefore, we need to use the Auto Data Prep node to reformat these fields.

Steps to Build Logistic Model 1

  1. Open SPSS Modeler and create a new stream. Name the stream “Airline_Regression.”

  2. Add the data source file “AirlineRecommendation.sav” to the stream.

  3. Add a Type node to the stream and connect it to the data source. Open the Type node settings.

  4. 256. Double-check the field names, measurement scales, and roles for accuracy.

  5. Set the role of the field recommendation as Target. All other fields should be set as Input.

  6. Perform replacement using the Filter node to replace zero values in the price sensitivity field with missing values (see Chapter 5 for reference).

  7. Perform imputation using SuperNodes as described earlier (see Chapter 5 for reference). After this step, you should have a SuperNode named Missing Value Imputation for handling missing values.

  8. Add another Type node to the stream and connect it to the SuperNode Missing Value Imputation. Open the Type node settings and double-check the fields, measurements, and roles.

  9. Add a Partition node to the stream and connect it to the Type node. Open the Partition node settings.

  10. Select Train, test, and validation and set the training partition size to 60%, the testing partition size to 20%, and the validation partition size to 20% (refer to the Data Partition step for more details).

  11. Click Apply, then click OK.

  12. Add an Auto Data Prep node to the stream and connect it to the Partition node.

  13. Under Settings > Prepare Inputs & Target, check the box for Reorder nominal fields to have the smallest category first, largest last and uncheck all other boxes. This ensures proper numeric formatting for categorical input fields required to run the Logistic node.

  14. Click Apply and then Analyze Data.

  15. 257. Add another Type node to the stream and connect it to the Auto Data Prep node. Open the Type node settings.

  16. Confirm that all categorical input fields have been transformed (I use a _t suffix to denote transformed fields).

  17. From the Modeling group, add a Logistic node to the stream. Name it Logistic 1 and connect it to the Type node. Open the Logistic node settings.

  18. Under the Model tab, select Use partition data and Build model for each split.

  19. Select Binomial for the Procedure.

  20. Choose Forward Stepwise for the Method.

  21. 258. Select and add all categorical inputs to the model. The Base Category column shows the reference level for these categorical inputs. You can change it to either the First or Last level. For this example, leave the setting as First for all fields.

  22. Under the Analyze tab, select Calculate predictor importance.

  23. Click Apply and Run.

  24. SPSS Modeler will run the analysis and add the model nugget (result node) to the stream. If there are errors during the run, the software will display an error message.

  25. From the Output group, add an Analysis node to the stream and connect it to the model nugget Regression 1. This node will compare the model's performance between the training and test samples. Open the Analysis node settings.

  26. 259. Under the Analysis tab, select the following options:

    • Coincidence matrices (for symbolic targets)

    • Performance evaluation

    • Evaluation metric

    • Confidence figures

    • Separate by partition

  27. Click Apply and Run.

The output from the Analysis 1 node provides us with key metrics as follows:

  • Coincidence matrix: Equivalent to the confusion matrix, showing true positives (TP), true negatives (TN), false positives (FP), and false negatives (FN). This matrix is crucial because it allows us to calculate important model fit metrics.

  • Correct percent: Equivalent to prediction accuracy (ACC).

  • 260. Wrong percent: Equivalent to the misclassification rate (MR).

  • Evaluation metrics: Includes AUC (area under the curve), also known as the ROC index, and the Gini coefficient.

Using the formulas described in Chapter 6, we can calculate additional metrics, such as sensitivity, specificity, and F1 score, using the information from the confusion matrix.

Now that we know how to build a logistic regression model and extract model fit metrics from SPSS Modeler outputs, the next step is to build the remaining three logistic regression models and compare them to identify the champion model.

Logistic Models 2, 3, and 4

Follow the same steps outlined earlier to set up and configure Logistic Regression models 2, 3, and 4, using the configurations and nodes described in Table 7.20. Below are the specific configurations for each model.

Logistic 2:

  • Use the dataset with missing values (no imputation).

  • No normalization.

  • Configure the Logistic node: Binomial model with the Forward Stepwise method.

Logistic 3:

  • Use the Auto Data Prep node with the objective to “Balance speed and accuracy.”

  • Perform automatic data preparation, data imputation, and standardization (without outlier handling).

  • Configure the Logistic node: Binomial model with the Forward Stepwise method.

Logistic 4:

  • Use the Auto Data Prep node with the objective to “Optimize for accuracy.”

  • Perform automatic data preparation, data imputation, standardization, and outlier handling.

  • Configure the Logistic node: Binomial model with the Forward Stepwise method.

Model Fit Assessment

264. Based on the validation results, the prediction accuracy seems slightly low at 76.8%, with a misclassification rate (MR) of around 23.2%. However, examining sensitivity and specificity provides more insight. The model demonstrates relatively strong sensitivity at 89.3%, indicating it can effectively predict positive cases (i.e., recommending the airline). On the other hand, specificity is moderate at 63%, suggesting the model struggles to predict negative cases (i.e., not recommending the airline).

The confusion matrix shows that false positives (FP) are higher than false negatives (FN). The F1 score, which balances sensitivity and precision, is 80.2%, which is acceptable. Lastly, the Gini coefficient of 0.667 is considered good.

Overall, while MR and ACC alone may indicate a lower model fit, examining other metrics, such as sensitivity, specificity, F1 score, and Gini coefficient, gives a clearer understanding of the model's performance.

Before making a final conclusion about model fit, we should review the ROC and Lift charts for confirmation. Using the validation sample:

  • The ROC chart (Figure 7.14) shows that the model lies between the baseline (diagonal line) and the perfect-fit model (upper left corner). With an AUC index of 0.833, the model's performance is acceptable (an ROC index of 0.9 or higher indicates a strong model fit).

  • The Lift chart (Figure 7.15) shows that with 20% of the dataset, the Lift value is 1.6, meaning the model captures 32% of positive cases (1.6 times more than using no model), which is also considered an acceptable fit.

C​onclusion

These charts confirm the earlier results. If the objective is to predict positive cases (airline recommendations), this model performs well with a sensitivity of 89.3%. However, it does a poorer job of predicting non-recommendations (negatives).

Ultimately, when faced with mixed results, the decision on whether the model is acceptable depends on the business context. Alternatively, further refinements can be made by reconfiguring the algorithm or selecting a different one.

267. For example, while the results indicate that destination state has a significant effect overall, none of the individual states show significant effects on the target field when compared to the reference level (State of Alabama). As a result, we do not interpret the effect of this predictor.

The interpretation method follows the approach previously described for each predictor (we will not interpret the intercept, as it has no practical implications, even though it is necessary for the regression equation). To simplify interpretation, I have grouped interval predictors and nominal/binary predictors separately.

Key points to remember:

  • An odds ratio greater than 1 indicates a positive effect.

  • An odds ratio less than 1 indicates a negative effect.

As you can see, interpreting interval predictors is relatively straightforward, while interpreting nominal and binary predictors requires more care. Additionally, odds ratios greater than 1 are generally easier to interpret than those below 1.

Variable Importance

An important question to consider is: How important are the significant predictors, and which are more influential than others? To answer this, we use the variable importance chart found in the Model tab of the model nugget Logistic 1 (Figure 7.17).

The results indicate that travel purpose is the most important predictor, followed by airline status, age, and arrival delay. Conversely, flight cancellation, price sensitivity, and destination state are among the least important predictors.

As shown in the chart, the importance scores range from 0 to 1 and are scale-independent. Thus, they provide useful insights into the relative importance of each predictor. These findings can assist airline executives in developing marketing and promotion strategies to improve services and attract more passengers.

How to Run the Analysis Node With Multiple Models?

268. As mentioned earlier, SPSS Modeler does not have a specific node for comparing selected metrics among all models, like the Model Comparison node in SAS Enterprise Miner. However, there is a way to connect an Analysis node to multiple model nuggets and compare metrics across models. I’ll walk you through the process, but keep the following restrictions in mind:

  • Single connection limit: You cannot simply add an Analysis node and connect it to all model nuggets at once. SPSS Modeler will give an error message because the Analysis node can only connect to one model nugget at a time.

  • Detaching model nuggets: To connect multiple model nuggets to the Analysis node, you must first detach the model nuggets (except for the first one) from the Partition or Type node. This is because each model nugget can only connect to one preceding node. Next, connect the model nuggets to one another in sequence, and then connect the final nugget in that sequence to the Analysis node before running the analysis.

  • Copying models and nuggets: If you copy models and nuggets from another stream, ensure the model node and the model nugget remain connected after copying.

  • Identical field names: Fields in all model nuggets must have identical names. If any model has been transformed in a way that changes the field names, it cannot be compared with other models in the sequence, as this will cause SPSS Modeler to produce an error message. This restriction limits the utility of this method for model comparison purposes.

  • Reconfiguring models: You can still reconfigure the models and rerun them as needed.

Figure 7.18 provides an example of a stream that compares multiple models using this approach. For better organization, it is recommended to arrange the model nodes and nuggets in sequence for easy tracking. As shown, all model nodes remain connected to their nuggets and the Partition node, but the nuggets must be connected to one another sequentially.

Example: Compare Multiple Models

As mentioned, we built four logistic regression models for this dataset. However, keep in mind that Logistic 1 and Logistic 2 only include data transformation for categorical fields, while Logistic 3 and Logistic 4 involve transformation for all fields. As a result, the field names in Logistic 1 and Logistic 2 differ from those in Logistic 3 and Logistic 4. This difference prevents us from directly comparing all models together using this approach, since SPSS Modeler requires identical field names for model comparison, and it will return an error if they differ.

269. In this case, I will guide you on how to compare Logistic 1 and Logistic 2. You can follow the same steps to compare Logistic 3 and Logistic 4 separately.

In the output, you may notice that the models appear under the predicted target names instead of the model names. Specifically:

  • Logistic 1 will appear as $L-Recommend the airline

  • Logistic 2 will appear as $L1-Recommend the airline

These names can be difficult to remember and track, especially when presenting results. To change the model names in the output, we can edit the field names using the Filter node. I’ll show you how to do this in the steps as follows.

Steps to Compare Logistic Models 1 and 2:

  1. Start with the stream Airline_Regression that we created earlier.

  2. Detach the model nugget for Logistic 2 from the Type node. To do this, hover over the connector, right-click, and select Delete Connection.

  3. Connect the model nugget for Logistic 1 to the model nugget for Logistic 2.

  4. Add a Filter node to the stream and connect it to the model nugget for Logistic 2.

  5. Open the Filter node settings. (Note that this screen will only appear after you have already run the Logistic 1 and Logistic 2 models, which we did earlier in this chapter.)

  6. In the settings, change $L-Recommend the airline to Logistic 1, and change $L1-Recommend the airline to Logistic 2.

  7. 270. Click Apply and OK.

  8. Add an Analysis node from the Output group and connect it to the Filter node.

  9. Open the Analysis node settings and configure it as done previously.

  10. Click Apply and Run.

Figure 7.19 shows the results of the Analysis node, which presents three key outputs as follows:

  • Individual models: Analysis outputs for both models, as shown previously. Since we changed the names, the models are now displayed with the desired labels.

  • Agreement between two models: The level of similarity in predictions between the two models. In this case, the models show a high level of agreement, with more than 98% similarity.

  • Evaluation metrics: A comparison of the models based on AUC and the Gini coefficient. As mentioned earlier, Logistic 1 shows slightly better results than Logistic 2.

Please note that we still need to calculate other fit metrics, such as sensitivity and specificity, separately using the confusion matrix.

We can also add an Evaluation Graph node to the model nugget for Logistic 2 and run it to produce an ROC comparison chart or Lift comparison chart for both models. In this case, the ROC and Lift charts for both models are nearly identical, so the difference is not noticeable in the charts (Figure 7.20 and Figure 7.21). However, in other cases, these chart comparisons could be useful. Regardless, we can always review the AUC (ROC index) and Lift score to compare the models.271.

272.

C​o​nclusion

This approach offers an alternative method to compare metrics among models using a single Analysis node. However, it has several limitations:

  • It requires modifications to the stream, which prevents reconfiguring the models within the stream.

  • The restriction on identical field names makes it difficult to compare models that use transformed data.

  • Some important metrics still need to be calculated manually based on each model's confusion matrix.

My recommendation is to use separate Analysis nodes for each model and extract the necessary metrics. In cases where field names are identical across models, this method can still be useful for generating ROC and Lift charts for multiple models.

Chapter Summary

Regression is one of the most widely used machine learning algorithms due to its simplicity in implementation and ease of interpreting results. Regression methods allow us to predict the value of a target variable based on multiple predictors. Linear regression is an association model used for continuous target variables while logistic regression is a classification model used for binary target variables. The key characteristic of regression methods is the assumption of a linear relationship. In linear regression, the equation represents a linear relationship between the target variable and the predictors, whereas in logistic regression, the equation represents a linear relationship between the logit value of the target variable and the predictors.

Regression analysis is widely applied across fields such as economics, finance, healthcare, aviation, and social sciences to make predictions and derive insights from data.

This chapter covers the fundamental concepts and techniques of regression, including regression equations, estimation methods, model selection, assumptions, model fit metrics, and interpreting outputs. We also demonstrate how to perform both linear and logistic regressions on actual datasets using SPSS Modeler. This chapter provides detailed, hands-on examples of model training, result presentation, model comparison, champion model selection, and regression equation interpretation.

While regression offers numerous advantages, such as providing a straightforward approach to making predictions and being interpretable, it also has limitations. Regression assumes a linear relationship between variables, and violations of this assumption may lead to inaccurate predictions. Additionally, regression models are sensitive to outliers and missing data, which can affect model performance.

Overall, regression is a valuable tool in data mining for understanding and predicting relationships between variables, but it is crucial to carefully assess its assumptions and limitations to ensure reliable results.

Introduction

This chapter focuses on the decision tree method, a popular machine learning technique that presents the hierarchical structure of variables in tree form using logical rules. The tree consists of nodes that split into two or more branches based on conditions that best separate individuals into classes. It is one of the most widely used machine learning methods due to its ease of implementation and interpretation. The tree structure visually demonstrates relationships among variables through nodes and branches, making it intuitive to understand. Additionally, decision trees are capable of detecting nonlinear relationships.

In this chapter, we will explore the advantages and disadvantages of decision trees, enabling us to compare them with other machine learning methods. The four common types of decision trees—CART (Classification and Regression Tree), CHAID (Chi-squared Automatic Interaction Detector), C5.0, and QUEST (Quick, Unbiased, Efficient, Statistical Tree)—will be discussed. We will examine their characteristics and differences, and I will demonstrate how to build these trees using SPSS Modeler, including the tree pruning process.

276. Since decision trees are non-parametric and based on logical rules, their theoretical foundation differs significantly from regression methods. Rather than relying on mathematical equations, we follow the branches of the tree to observe how predictors correlate with the target variable. Although mathematical algorithms are still used to build the tree hierarchy, I will focus on explaining the method in a simple and practical way so that you can understand how it works without delving too deeply into the underlying algorithms.

What Is a Decision Tree? How Does it Work?

A decision tree is a highly popular machine learning method, frequently used in decision-making processes and data mining projects. It is a non-parametric and nonlinear method. Decision tree models offer the advantage of conceptual simplicity, making them easy to understand while also accommodating nonlinear associations between predictors and the target variable. The tree is represented as a flowchart, visually illustrating the relationships among variables, which makes it easy to comprehend and explain—even in complex processes. This is a significant advantage, as many other machine learning algorithms lack this level of interpretability.

Now, let's explore a simple example of a decision tree shown in Figure 8.1. Suppose we want to predict the likelihood of passengers purchasing an airline ticket for a trip, based on factors such as ticket price, family emergency, and hotel price. The flowchart captures the decision-making process or the rules that define the relationship between the passenger's decision (the target variable) and these factors (the predictors). Let's examine the tree structure.

  • The primary factor is ticket price, which forms the root node. The flowchart shows that if the ticket price is high, the next factor to consider is the family emergency. If there is a family emergency, the passenger will decide to purchase the ticket, even if the price is 277. high. However, in the absence of an emergency, the ticket will not be purchased since the trip can be postponed.

  • If the ticket price is medium, the next factor to consider is the hotel price. A high hotel price will likely deter the passengers from purchasing the ticket, as they may prefer to wait for a better opportunity. Conversely, if the hotel price is low, it represents a good deal, and the passenger will proceed to purchase the ticket.

  • Finally, if the ticket price is low, it is considered a good deal, and the passenger will purchase the ticket and proceed with the trip without needing to consider other factors.

As you can observe, the decision tree presents the decision-making process in a straightforward and logical manner. It is easy to follow and understand the relationships among variables based on these rules. The tree provides us with a set of rules that can be used to make predictions. Thus, the decision tree is a logical, rule-based method rather than a statistical or mathematical one. The flowchart allows us to create a model that predicts the ticket purchasing decision based on these predictors. When properly trained and validated with enough data, it can predict the purchasing decision (purchase vs. not purchase) with good predictive power.

A decision tree represents a hierarchical structure of variables, consisting of the root node, parent nodes, child nodes, and leaf nodes:

  • The root node is at the top of the tree and contains the entire dataset.

  • A parent node is any node that splits into child nodes, forming branches. Whether a node is considered a parent or child depends on the perspective of interpretation.

  • Any node that falls under another node is considered a child node while the node directly preceding it is the parent node. This means a node can be both a child node to one parent and a parent node to other child nodes.

  • The final nodes of the decision tree are called leaf nodes or leaves. For each leaf, a decision is made and applied to all observations within that node. In predictive modeling, the decision is the predicted value.

In our example, the tree hierarchy is as follows:

  • Ticket price serves as the root node, and family emergency and hotel price are child nodes, each of which splits into two branches.

  • Family emergency is also a parent node, with two child nodes: purchase and not purchase.

  • The rounded rectangle nodes are the leaves, representing the final classification decisions (purchase or not purchase).

Basic Concepts of Decision Trees

Given the number of new terms introduced in this chapter, Table 8.1 provides an overview of the basic concepts in decision tree methods along with their descriptions.

TABLE 8.1 Basic Concepts of Decision Trees Return to text.⏎

Terms

Descriptions

Decision tree

Decision tree is a logical rule-based method that organizes variables in a hierarchical structure, consisting of a root node, parent nodes, and child nodes.

Root node

A root node is at the beginning of a tree. It represents the initial decision based on a specific feature that has the most significant impact on the target variable. Starting from the root node, the dataset is partitioned based on different features, and subsequently, these subgroups are further divided at each decision node located beneath the root node.

Splitting

Splitting is a process of dividing a node into two or more sub-nodes.

Splitting criterion

Splitting criterion is a measure used to evaluate and select the best predictor to split the data at each node of the tree. It is a measure of impurity or variance reduction.

Decision node

When a sub-node is divided into additional sub-nodes, it is referred to as a decision node.

Leaf node

Nodes that do not split are called leaf nodes. They represent the output or the predicted value/class for the specific subgroup of data that reaches that node.

Pruning

Removing the sub-nodes of a parent node is called pruning. It is a technique used to simplify the decision tree by removing nodes that do not significantly improve its performance on the validation set. A tree is grown through splitting and shrunk through pruning.

Branch or subtree

A branch or a subtree is a sub-section of a decision tree.

Parent node and child node

These terms are relative in nature. Any node situated below another node is typically referred to as a child node or sub-node while the node preceding these child nodes is commonly known as the parent node.

Recursive partitioning

Recursive partitioning denotes an iterative procedure involving the division of data into partitions, followed by further splitting along each branch.

Classification and Regression Tree (CART)

CART is a binary tree algorithm that repeatedly splits a parent node into two child nodes. It can be used for both classification and regression models. CART uses measures like Gini impurity or variance reduction to determine splits.

Chi-squared Automatic Interaction Detection (CHAID)

CHAID is a non-parametric method used to create decision trees by recursively splitting the data into homogeneous subgroups based on categorical predictors. It uses the chi-squared test to assess independence between variables and identify significant splits. CHAID is commonly used for categorical variables and allows for more than two child nodes at each split.

C5.0 tree

C5.0 algorithm is designed for classification tasks and uses the information gain ratio to determine splits. It builds scalable, interpretable decision trees and uses advanced pruning techniques to prevent overfitting. C5.0 is known for being an improvement over its predecessor, C4.5, with faster performance and more flexibility.

Quick, Unbiased, Efficient, Statistical Tree (QUEST)

QUEST is a binary decision tree algorithm used primarily for classification. It uses statistical methods to ensure unbiased splits and is designed to handle large datasets efficiently. It offers quick, unbiased decisions and reduces the bias that can sometimes occur in other decision tree algorithms when dealing with continuous predictors.

How Does Node Splitting Work?

278. From the example above, we see how a tree is structured based on the hierarchy of decisions made by passengers. The process of node splitting is crucial to constructing that tree. So, how does node splitting work?

Node splitting is a key process in constructing the hierarchical structure of a decision tree. It determines how the data should be partitioned at each level of the tree. During this process, the algorithm selects a variable, and the corresponding node is split into two or more branches based on a condition that best separates individuals into classes.

  • If the variable is categorical, the branches represent different classes.

  • If the variable is interval-based (continuous), the branches represent specific ranges.

279. At each split, a separation condition is applied to determine how the parent node is split into child nodes. This continues until a stopping rule is met. This overall process is called recursive partitioning.

Recursive Partitioning Steps

  1. Selecting a splitting criterion: At each node, the algorithm selects a variable and a corresponding splitting criterion to partition the data into child nodes. The splitting criterion depends on the target variable's scale and may include measures such as the F-test, chi-square test, Gini impurity, or Entropy.

  2. Splitting the data: The selected criterion is used to divide the node into two or more child nodes, with each child node representing a branch from the current node in the tree.

  3. Stopping criteria: The algorithm checks if any stopping conditions are met, such as follows:

    • Reaching a maximum tree depth

    • Having a minimum number of samples per leaf

    • Achieving a certain level of impurity reduction

  4. Recursive process: If the stopping criteria are not met, the process continues recursively for each branch. The child nodes become new parent nodes, and the process repeats.

  5. Leaf nodes: When a stopping criterion is satisfied or no further meaningful splits are possible, the process ends, and the final nodes are called leaf nodes. These leaf nodes represent the final predictions for the target variable.

The recursive partitioning process continues until all stopping criteria are met, or until the tree becomes fully grown. However, a fully grown tree may result in overfitting, where the model captures noise and specific details of the training data, which can lead to poor predictive power on unseen data. To address this issue, tree pruning can be applied to simplify the tree by removing branches that do not contribute significantly to the model's performance. Pruning techniques will be covered later in this chapter.

In summary, recursive partitioning in decision trees is a top-down approach that begins with the entire dataset and recursively divides it into smaller, more homogeneous subsets. This process is efficient and enables decision trees to handle both categorical and continuous variables, making them powerful and interpretable models for data mining.

Do Missing Values Have Effects on Decision Trees?

In traditional statistical studies, missing values are a significant concern because they can represent missing information in the data and negatively affect the results. Regression methods are particularly sensitive to missing values, as they typically require a complete dataset to build models with a good fit. Additionally, missing values can lead to a loss of information and introduce bias into the data.

However, decision trees are a non-parametric method based on logical rules, and they handle missing values much more effectively. Since decision trees are constructed by splitting parent nodes into multiple child nodes, missing values have a less significant impact on the process of building the tree. Decision trees can naturally handle missing values through several mechanisms.

280. Ways Decision Trees Handle Missing Values:

  1. Splitting criteria with missing values: Decision trees use different splitting criteria, such as Gini impurity or Entropy, to determine the best variable and threshold for splitting the data at each node. When a variable contains missing values for certain data points, the algorithm can treat these missing values as a separate category or group. Data points with missing values may traverse down both branches of the split, allowing the tree to calculate impurity or error based on the available data. This way, decision trees can leverage the information from non-missing values to make decisions, even when some data points are incomplete.

  2. Surrogate splitting: Surrogate splitting is another method used by decision trees to handle missing values. When the primary split contains missing values, the decision tree algorithm identifies alternative splits (or surrogates) that closely mimic the primary split based on available data. The surrogate split is then applied when the primary split cannot be used, effectively handling the missing data.

  3. Using imputation: Some decision tree implementations support the imputation of missing values, where missing data are replaced with estimated values. We have covered imputation techniques in Chapter 5.

  4. Creating multiple branches: If a data point has missing values for multiple variables, the decision tree may create multiple branches from the current node to account for different combinations of missing and non-missing values. The algorithm evaluates each branch separately, considering the available data for each data point.

  5. Handling missing values during prediction: When making predictions on new data with missing values, the decision tree can still generate predictions by following the appropriate branches based on the available values. If a data point has missing values for multiple variables, the tree may traverse down multiple paths to reach the leaf nodes. The predictions from these paths are then combined to make the final prediction.

It is important to note that some data mining software programs, such as SPSS Modeler, include built-in features that handle missing values more efficiently during decision tree modeling. It is recommended to use software with these built-in algorithms for the best results.

Advantages and Disadvantages of Decision Tree Methods

Decision tree is a very popular method in data mining. It is a non-parametric method that can detect nonlinear relationships. It can be used with various measurement scales and is not sensitive to missing values or outliers. The tree structure is logical and easy to understand and interpret. Since we use a strategy that requires developing multiple models using different methods and configurations, it is important to understand the advantages and disadvantages of decision trees, which allows us to compare this method with the regression methods we covered in Chapter 7 and other 281. more advanced methods we will cover later. I summarize the key advantages and disadvantages of this method as follows:

Advantages of Decision Trees

  • Interpretability: Decision trees provide a transparent and intuitive representation of the decision-making process. The tree's hierarchical structure is easy to understand and interpret, making it a valuable tool for explaining the predictions to non-experts.

  • Handling non-linearity and complex relationships: By using decision trees, researchers can effectively capture nonlinear relationships and complex interactions between variables through the hierarchical structure.

  • Flexibility with data types: Decision trees can be used to build either association models or classification models, making them versatile and suitable for a wide range of applications. They can also work with both continuous and categorical predictors.

  • Irrelevant features: Decision trees are useful to model irrelevant variables in the data since they focus on variables that are more informative for splitting the data.

  • Scalability: Large datasets are handled more efficiently in decision trees, which do not require high computing power.

  • Handling missing values: Due to the nature of the recursive partitioning process, decision trees are able to handle missing values effectively through the splitting process.

  • Ensemble methods: Decision trees can be combined using ensemble methods like Random Forests and Gradient Boosting, which often lead to improved predictive performance and reduced overfitting.

  • Providing variable importance: A relative variable importance plot is available in a decision tree's output, which makes it easier for us to identify important predictors.

Disadvantages of Decision Trees

  • Overfitting: Decision trees are sensitive to overfitting, especially when the tree is deep and complex.

  • Instability and variance: Small changes in the data can lead to significantly different tree structures, which results in high variance in the predictions.

  • Bias toward dominant classes: In classification models with imbalanced datasets, decision trees may be biased toward the majority class, which leads to suboptimal performance in minority classes.

  • Difficulty handling numeric outliers: Decision trees are sensitive to the scale of continuous variables, and outliers can have a disproportionate influence on the tree's structure and predictions.

  • Global optimum vs. local optimum: The greedy nature of the decision tree algorithm may lead to suboptimal splits at individual nodes, even though they contribute to the overall best split.

  • Lack of coefficients: Unlike regression, the output of a decision tree model does not provide coefficients for evaluating the effects of predictors on the target variable. These effects must be evaluated through the tree structure and the probability values, which could be challenging to understand.

Despite their limitations, decision trees remain a valuable and widely used machine learning method, especially for data mining projects that require interpretability, handling nonlinear relationships, and dealing with both categorical and continuous variables. However, to address some of the drawbacks, techniques like pruning, ensemble methods, and careful hyperparameter tuning are often applied to improve the model performance.

Tree Pruning

282. Pruning is a crucial step in ensuring a decision tree model has good predictive power. Pruning involves removing redundant subtrees and replacing them with leaf nodes. Large trees with many branches and layers can lead to overfitting, which occurs when the model performs well on training data but poorly on new data. Additionally, large trees are difficult to interpret and understand. These trees often use the same predictors to construct the hierarchy, repeatedly splitting nodes to create numerous branches in an attempt to improve model fit. However, this process can result in overly complex trees that only fit the training data, leading to overfitting.

Pruning helps to prevent overfitting by simplifying the tree, making it more generalized to new datasets, without sacrificing model accuracy. Furthermore, a pruned tree is easier to understand and interpret. Figure 8.2 illustrates the process of decision tree pruning.

The process of tree pruning consists of six steps:

  1. Growing the full tree: The first step is to grow the decision tree to its maximum depth or until a stopping criterion is met. During this stage, the algorithm recursively partitions the data and creates branches and nodes based on a chosen splitting criterion.

  2. Evaluating node importance: After growing the full tree, assess the importance of each node in improving model performance. Nodes that contribute little to predictive accuracy or are not statistically significant are candidates for pruning.

  3. Cost-complexity pruning: Cost-complexity pruning, also known as minimal cost-complexity pruning, is a popular pruning method. It introduces a complexity parameter (alpha) that balances model accuracy and complexity. The algorithm evaluates the impact of removing each node and calculates a cost-complexity score for the subtree rooted at that node.

  4. 283. Selecting the optimal pruning level: The algorithm iteratively prunes nodes with the smallest cost-complexity score while evaluating model performance on a validation set. Pruning continues until further reductions result in a significant drop in predictive performance. The optimal pruning level corresponds to the subtree that provides the best balance between accuracy and simplicity.

  5. Pruning the tree: Once the optimal pruning level is determined, the tree is pruned by removing nodes and branches corresponding to subtrees above the selected level. The resulting pruned tree is a simplified version of the full tree.

Pruning helps control overfitting by reducing the complexity of the decision tree, thereby improving its predictive power. It also enhances model interpretability by providing a more concise representation of the decision-making process. However, pruning is a data-driven process, and the optimal pruning level may vary depending on the specific dataset. Regular validation is essential to determine the best pruning strategy for each model.

Types of Decision Tree Pruning

Decision tree pruning can be classified into two types: pre-pruning and post-pruning.

  • Pre-pruning (also known as the Early Stopping Rule): Pre-pruning prevents the growth of a tree beyond a specific size or depth based on certain measures like the Gini index or entropy. In this method, the tree-building process is halted when a pruning condition is met at a node. If the condition is satisfied, the subtree is pruned by replacing the decision node with a leaf node. Otherwise, the tree continues to grow. Pre-pruning is faster and more efficient, as it prevents the creation of overly complex subtrees that may overfit the training data. However, pre-pruning can stop the tree's growth prematurely based on the stopping condition.

  • Post-pruning: In post-pruning, the entire tree is grown first, and then subtrees are pruned from the bottom-up. Starting from the bottom decision nodes, measures such as Gini impurity or information gain are used to decide whether to keep a decision node or replace it with a leaf node.

Manual vs. Automatic Pruning

  • Manual pruning: Manual pruning is generally not recommended for data mining projects because it relies on the researcher's judgment, which can introduce bias. Manual pruning also requires a clear justification for removing a subtree, which may not always be evident. For example, how do we know which branches are redundant to remove, and how do we justify that decision? Mistakes in manual pruning can lead to poorer model fit or render the tree ineffective. While manual pruning may be feasible for simple trees, it is impractical for large trees with many nodes and branches. It also defeats the purpose of mining large datasets.

  • Automatic pruning: The recommended approach is automatic pruning. This involves setting specific criteria for tree development and subtree selection, allowing the software to perform pruning based on those configurations. Typically, you define how the software should select and assess subtrees and whether to apply cross-validation. The software then uses search algorithms to find the best tree that meets these criteria and requirements.

Different Types of Decision Trees

284. As demonstrated in the previous example, how a node is split is crucial to developing a good decision tree model. In data mining, decision trees are derived from data, not from common sense or business rules. Therefore, having valid splitting rules is essential to producing a decision tree model with strong predictive power. Splitting algorithms allow us to categorize different types of decision trees.

Over time, many types of decision tree algorithms have been developed. In this book, I introduce four tree algorithms that are widely used in data science and data mining projects:

  • CART

  • Chi-Squared Automatic Interaction Detection (CHAID)

  • C5.0

  • QUEST

I will provide a general overview of these trees, focusing on their splitting rules, pruning methods, and the appropriate scenarios for using each. As always, I will avoid mathematical formulations and emphasize practical applications.

Classification and Regression Tree (CART)

CART is a popular decision tree method developed by Breiman (1984). For more detailed information, you can refer to their book, Classification and Regression Trees. In this explanation, I will skip the mathematical details and focus on practical applications.

CART is a binary tree, meaning that it repeatedly splits a parent node into two child nodes. This process can be used for both categorical (classification) and continuous (regression) target variables. CART is widely employed in machine learning due to its simplicity, interpretability, and effectiveness.

Binary Recursive Splitting

CART uses a binary recursive splitting approach. At each node of the tree, the algorithm selects a feature and a threshold to split the data into two subsets. For categorical variables, CART performs multi-way splits by creating branches for each category, while for continuous variables, it identifies a threshold for splitting.

Splitting Criteria

  • For classification models, CART typically uses Gini impurity as the splitting criterion. Gini impurity measures the likelihood of incorrectly classifying a randomly chosen instance. The algorithm selects splits that minimize impurity.

  • 285. For regression models, CART uses variance reduction as the splitting criterion, with least squared deviation (LSD) being the common measure for variance. The goal is to find splits that reduce variance within the resulting subsets.

Most data mining software integrates both classification and regression capabilities in their CART implementation, so you don’t need to manually separate the two tree types.

Recursive Tree Building

The process of building the tree is recursive. After the initial split, the algorithm applies the same procedure to each resulting subset, continuing to split nodes until a stopping criterion is reached. Common stopping criteria include the following:

  • A minimum number of instances in a leaf node.

  • A maximum tree depth.

  • No further improvement in impurity or variance reduction.

Figure 8.3 illustrates what a binary tree looks like, where each parent node splits into exactly two child nodes.

Pruning

Once the tree is fully grown, it may be pruned to improve generalization and avoid overfitting. Pruning involves removing branches that do not significantly enhance predictive accuracy. CART typically uses cost-complexity pruning, which balances the complexity of the tree with its accuracy on a validation set.

Handling Missing Values

286. CART is capable of handling missing data. When a feature contains missing values, the algorithm distributes instances with missing data among child nodes based on the available information from other features.

Chi-Squared Automatic Interaction Detection (CHAID)

CHAID was developed by Kass in 1980. This method is based on the chi-square statistic, a non-parametric test used to examine differences between categorical variables. CHAID aims to identify significant relationships between variables by applying chi-squared tests for independence. The test produces a probability value (p-value) between 0 and 1. A chi-square value closer to 0 indicates a significant difference between the two variables while a value closer to 1 indicates no significant difference. Unlike CART, CHAID can split a parent node into more than two child nodes, making it useful for creating multi-way splits.

Splitting Rule

At each split, CHAID assesses the statistical significance of the relationships between predictor variables and the target variable using chi-squared tests. The algorithm seeks to create homogeneous groups, where the target variable is similar within each branch of the tree.

Handling Continuous and Categorical Variables

CHAID is primarily designed for categorical variables. While it works for both association and classification models, it requires categorical predictors, either ordinal or nominal. However, many software implementations of CHAID can accept continuous variables by automatically grouping values into ranges before growing the tree. Since Kass’ original algorithm, CHAID has evolved to handle continuous target variables by using the p-value from an F-test. A key distinction from CART is that CHAID can split a node into two or more child nodes, as illustrated in Figure 8.4, which depicts a multi-way tree.

Initial Split

CHAID starts with the entire dataset, selecting the predictor variable that has the most significant association with the target variable based on a chi-squared test for independence. The dataset is then split into subsets according to the chosen variable and its categories.

Recursive Splitting

The algorithm recursively splits each subset into smaller subsets by selecting the variables and categories that maximize the statistical association with the target variable. The process continues until a stopping criterion is met, such as reaching a maximum tree depth or having a minimum number of instances in a leaf node.

Handling Multi-Way Splits

CHAID can perform multi-way splits for categorical variables with more than two categories, creating branches for each category. This ability makes it well-suited for datasets with multiple categorical variables.

Merge Procedure for Pruning

287. After the tree is constructed, CHAID applies a merge procedure to prune the tree and simplify its structure. This process merges adjacent categories or nodes that do not significantly differ in terms of the target variable. The merge procedure helps prevent overfitting and produces a more interpretable final tree.

Handling Missing Values

CHAID handles missing values using surrogate splits. Missing values are treated as separate categories, and if a variable has missing data, CHAID identifies surrogate variables—alternative predictors that closely mimic the behavior of the primary variable. These surrogates act as backup rules when making decisions for instances with missing values.

C5.0 Tree

C5.0 is a powerful decision tree algorithm developed by Ross Quinlan in 1993. Primarily designed for classification models, C5.0 can also handle association models. The algorithm uses the information gain or gain ratio criterion to select the best attributes for node splitting, creating a tree structure that optimally classifies or predicts the target variable. C5.0 is known for its efficiency, scalability, and ability to handle both categorical and continuous variables. Additionally, it incorporates advanced pruning techniques to improve model interpretability and prevent overfitting, making it a widely 288. used and effective tool for predictive modeling. It is considered an improvement over its predecessor, C4.5, offering faster performance and greater flexibility.

Entropy and Information Gain

C5.0 uses the concept of entropy to measure the impurity or disorder in a dataset. Entropy quantifies the uncertainty associated with a random variable. Information gain is then employed to find the best variable for splitting the dataset at each node. It measures the reduction in entropy that results from splitting the data based on a particular variable.

Splitting Criteria

The algorithm evaluates various predictors and selects the one that maximizes information gain or other splitting criteria like gain ratio. These criteria help determine which variable best improves the homogeneity of the target variable's distribution across the resulting child nodes. The goal is to partition the data into subsets that are more homogeneous in terms of the target variable.

Tree Construction

The dataset is divided into subsets based on the selected variable, and the process is recursively applied to each subset. The tree continues to grow until a stopping criterion is met, such as reaching a maximum tree depth or having a minimum number of instances in a leaf node.

Handling Continuous and Categorical Variables

While C5.0 is primarily designed for building classification trees, it can handle both continuous and categorical variables. For continuous variables, the algorithm determines optimal split points based on information gain. It can also handle categorical variables with multiple levels, finding the best way to split the categories for maximum information gain.

Pruning

Once the tree is fully grown, it may be pruned to avoid overfitting. The C5.0 algorithm uses a combination of cost-complexity pruning and reduced-error pruning to enhance the tree's ability to generalize to new data.

Handling Missing Values

C5.0 handles missing values in the dataset using surrogate splits. These are alternative rules that serve as backups when the primary variable for splitting has missing values for certain instances.

Quest (Quick, Unbiased, Efficient, Statistical Tree)

QUEST is a decision tree algorithm developed by Loh and Shih in 1997. It is designed for building trees in classification models, with a particular emphasis on handling large datasets efficiently. QUEST is known for its speed and the robust statistical foundation that guides its split decisions.

289.

Overview of QUEST

QUEST operates by using a statistical approach to construct decision trees. The algorithm iteratively selects variables and split points based on statistical criteria, aiming to maximize homogeneity within the branches while minimizing statistical impurity. Unlike traditional tree algorithms, QUEST performs simultaneous tests on multiple variables at each node, allowing for efficient and unbiased selection of the best split. The algorithm focuses on statistical significance and quick tree construction, adapting its structure to the complexity of the data. This makes QUEST particularly useful in situations where interpretability and statistical validity are key.

Binary Tree Structure

QUEST generates a binary tree, meaning each internal node splits into exactly two child nodes. This binary structure simplifies the decision-making process and enhances the efficiency of data separation.

Splitting Criteria

QUEST uses statistical measures to make splitting decisions. It often applies statistical tests, such as chi-squared tests or other association measures, to quantify the relationship between a potential splitting variable and the target classes. The goal is to maximize the statistical significance of each split, ensuring the resulting child nodes are as distinct as possible in terms of the target variable.

Recursive Binary Splitting

Similar to other decision tree algorithms, QUEST employs recursive binary splitting. The process begins with the entire dataset, selecting the predictor variable and split point that maximizes the statistical difference in the response variable. The data are then split into two subsets, and the process is repeated for each subset.

Stopping Criteria

The tree-building process continues until a predefined stopping criterion is met. Common stopping criteria include reaching a specified tree depth, having a minimum number of instances in a node, or other conditions designed to prevent overfitting. QUEST strives to find an optimal tree size based on statistical considerations.

Unbiased Approach

One of QUEST's main strengths is its unbiased approach to decision-making. The algorithm ensures that decisions are driven by statistical significance rather than biased criteria, providing an accurate and objective representation of the data.

Pruning

To avoid overfitting, QUEST incorporates pruning techniques. The pruning process uses a cost-complexity pruning strategy, where the algorithm evaluates the cost-complexity measure at various levels of tree complexity. It then selects a subtree that strikes an optimal balance between accuracy and simplicity.

Speed and Efficiency

290. A key feature of QUEST is its speed and efficiency, especially when dealing with large datasets. The algorithm is designed to be fast and unbiased, making it a suitable choice for applications where computational resources are limited or where processing time is critical.

Tree Algorithm Comparison

Table 8.2 highlights key differences between CART and CHAID decision trees. Overall, these two types of trees share many similarities, but they differ primarily in how nodes are split. As a reminder, CART uses a binary split algorithm, while CHAID uses a multi-split approach. Both methods can be applied to build either association or classification models. However, CART generally performs better with continuous or ordinal predictors while CHAID is more suited to categorical predictors. That said, most data mining software allows for a combination of predictor types.

Because of these differences in splitting algorithms, CART tends to produce smaller (narrower) but taller trees due to its binary splits, whereas CHAID typically results in larger but shorter trees because of its multi-split structure. Although CHAID may require more data than CART to train a model, it is generally less prone to overfitting. Some researchers suggest that pruning is unnecessary for CHAID, but I recommend pruning for both tree types to prevent overly large trees. We will explore examples of this in later sections.

291. Overall, each decision tree algorithm has its strengths and is suitable for different types of models and data. It is hard to speculate in advance which type of tree works better because they all have strengths and weaknesses. The choice of algorithm depends on the characteristics of the data and the specific requirements of the data mining. My recommendation is to build multiple trees using both types with different configurations and compare them to determine which tree works best for the data.

Example: Classification Model Using Decision Trees

292. In this example, we will build classification models for the Airline Recommendation dataset using decision trees. The target variable is whether a passenger recommends the airline, represented as a binary variable (Yes—recommend; No—not recommend). We will construct multiple decision tree models using different algorithms and assess which performs best for this dataset.

  • Dataset: AirlineRecommendation.sav

  • Target variable: Recommend (Flag: Yes/No)

To evaluate various algorithms under different conditions, I have developed the following scenarios to guide our decision tree model configurations:

  • Scenario 1: Compare a pruned model with a non-pruned model. This scenario examines the performance difference between pruning and not pruning a decision tree. It will help us determine whether pruning is a beneficial practice in predictive modeling. To simplify, we will use the CART algorithm for this scenario, as it is the most commonly used decision tree algorithm.

  • Scenario 2: Compare a model using imputed data, a model with missing values, and a model using the Auto Data Prep node (optimized for two objectives: accuracy and a balance between speed and accuracy). This scenario will assess how well decision tree algorithms handle missing data and whether it is advantageous to use non-transformed data for training. For consistency, we will use the CART algorithm again in this scenario.

  • Scenario 3: Compare different tree algorithms. In this scenario, we will build decision trees using four algorithms: CART, CHAID, C5.0, and QUEST. Each algorithm may be configured differently, so we will create more than four models. This scenario will help us identify which algorithm performs best for this dataset.

Starting Point

Since we have already covered key steps in data exploration, modification, and partitioning for this dataset in Chapter 7, we will not revisit them here. Instead, we will focus primarily on the modeling process. For details on those earlier steps, please refer to the previous chapters. The starting point for this example will begin with the Partition node, and from there, we will proceed with building the models.

Scenario 1: Pruned vs. Non-Pruned CART Models

In this scenario, we will build two CART models: one with pruning and one without. To ensure a fair comparison, we will use imputed data for both models.

293. Follow the steps below to build the CART models:

  1. Open SPSS Modeler.

  2. Create a new stream and name it “Airline_Tree.”

  3. Copy and paste the stream from “Airline_Regression” (as shown earlier) and double-check the nodes.

  4. Run the Data Audit nodes and verify the outputs, ensuring that the replacement and imputation tasks are correctly applied.

  5. Continue with the Partition node (recall that we partitioned the data with a 60–20–20 split for training, validation, and testing).

  6. From the Modeling group, add a C&R Tree node to the stream, name it C&R Tree 1 and connect it to the Partition node. Open the node settings.

  7. Under the Fields tab, confirm that the Target and Predictor fields are correct.

  8. Under the Build Options tab, select Objective from the left panel and check the box labeled “Build a single tree” (we are not using ensemble models in this chapter, as that will be covered in Chapter 10).

  9. In the Basics section, check the option Prune tree to avoid overfitting.

  10. Keep the default settings for Stopping Rules.

  11. Under the Model Options section, select “Calculate predictor importance.”

  12. Click Apply and run the model.

  13. SPSS Modeler will generate a model nugget labeled C&R Tree 1 which contains the results.

  14. Add an Analysis node to the stream and connect it to the model nugget C&R Tree 1. Open the Analysis node settings.

  15. Under the Analysis tab, select the following options: Performance evaluation, Evaluation metric, Confidence figures, and Separate by partition.

  16. Click Apply and run the analysis.

294. This will generate performance metrics for the pruned tree model. We will hold onto these results for comparison. Next, follow the same steps to create and configure a second tree, naming it C&R Tree 1 Non-Pruned. The only difference is that in Step 9, uncheck the box labeled Prune tree to avoid overfitting, instructing SPSS Modeler to build the full, unpruned tree. Run the analysis for this non-pruned model as well. The final stream configuration should resemble the setup shown above.

First, let's compare the trees generated by these two models. To extract the tree from the C&R Tree 1 model, open the model nugget labeled C&R Tree 1. Under the Viewer tab, you will find the tree. To make the tree structure easier to view, I displayed the tree with frequency information shown as a graph (Figure 8.5). Repeat this step for the model nugget C&R Tree 1 Non-Pruned. This will give us the full, unpruned tree (Figure 8.6).

So, how do these two trees differ in their hierarchical structure? As you can see, the non-pruned tree is larger, consisting of 34 nodes and 18 leaves. Analyzing each branch and node would be quite challenging due to its complexity. In contrast, the pruned tree is more compact and easier to interpret, with only 14 nodes and 8 leaves.

We compared the model fit metrics between the two trees using the validation results to assess their differences. The ACC, misclassification rate (MR), Gini coefficient, and AUC are directly 295. 296. provided by the outputs from the Analysis nodes. Sensitivity, specificity, and F1 score are calculated based on the confusion matrix. Using these results from the testing sample, the model comparison is presented in Table 8.3.

Scenario 2: CART Models with Missing Values vs. Imputed Data

In this scenario, we will compare a CART model that retains missing values with one that uses imputed data. Decision trees, in general, handle missing values better than regression algorithms. Since decision trees are rule-based rather than statistics-based, they do not typically require a complete dataset to function. Decision trees work by splitting data into distinct bins, so they offer various options for handling missing values without disrupting the model-building process. These options include ignoring missing values, using surrogate splits, treating missing values as a separate category, assigning a default value, or applying probability weighting. As such, using imputation does not necessarily provide any advantage when constructing a decision tree. In fact, imputation can introduce bias or increase prediction errors. Similarly, data normalization and outlier handling may not be necessary for decision tree algorithms.

In this scenario, we will compare three pruned CARTs, each constructed differently, and evaluate their performance:

  • C&R Tree 1: Uses imputed data without normalization or outlier handling.

  • C&R Tree 2: Retains missing values without normalization or outlier handling.

  • C&R Tree 3: Uses the Auto Data Prep node with the objective Optimize for accuracy, which imputes missing values, adjusts field scales, normalizes data, and handles outliers.

Follow the same steps we used previously to add C&R Tree 2 and C&R Tree 3 to the stream with the specified configurations. Your stream should resemble the one shown in the following diagram.

Run all three CART models and use the Analysis node to extract the model fit metrics for each. As before, you can obtain the ACC, MR, Gini coefficient, and AUC directly from the output of the Analysis node. To calculate sensitivity, specificity, and F1 score based on the confusion matrix, refer to the formulas discussed in Chapter 6. Make sure to use the results from the testing sample for model comparison. Table 8.4 presents the model comparison results for Scenario 2.

Furthermore, C&R Tree 2 (which retains missing values) slightly outperforms the other models, with higher accuracy, better sensitivity, and a higher F1 score. Scenario 3: CART vs. CHAID vs. C5.0 vs. QUEST

In this scenario, we will compare decision tree models developed using four different algorithms: CART, CHAID, C5.0, and QUEST. The objective is to identify which algorithm, and configurations work best for the Airline Recommendation dataset. From the previous scenarios, we determined that pruning the tree and retaining missing values in the dataset are the optimal choices for building decision trees. Therefore, in this scenario, we will only build pruned trees using data that contain the original missing values. For each algorithm, we will build two trees: one with the default settings for tree depth, pruning, and stopping rules and the other with modified settings to see if performance improves.

Below are the specific configurations for each model. Follow these settings to set up the trees. The models will then be compared to determine the best-performing model.

Given the close performance of these models, C&R Tree 2 is the better choice for demonstration.

303. As shown, the prediction ACC is below 80%, which is generally considered suboptimal. However, the model demonstrates excellent sensitivity (true positive rate) at 95.1%. The lower ACC can be attributed to poor specificity (true negative rate), meaning the model has a high false positive rate. Despite this, the F1 score—representing the balance between sensitivity and specificity—is considered acceptable. The Gini coefficient also indicates a good fit, and the ROC index shows an acceptable fit, as confirmed by the ROC curve for this model (Figure 8.7).

The Lift curve for the validation sample (Figure 8.8) shows that using 20% of the dataset yields a Lift value of 1.6, meaning the model can capture 1.6 times the positive cases compared to not using a model at all (1.6 × 20% = 32%). This is considered an acceptable result.

In summary, while the MR and ACC alone suggest a lower model fit, evaluating additional metrics such as sensitivity, F1 score, Gini coefficient, and ROC demonstrates that the overall fit of C&R Tree 2 is acceptable.

Conclusion

Although some fit metrics for this predictive model are considered acceptable, the model may not fully meet the expectations of airlines for predicting passenger recommendations. While the model performs well in predicting recommendation cases (positives), it struggles with predicting non-recommendation cases (negatives). The overall prediction ACC, particularly in reducing false positives, needs further improvement.

304. To illustrate how this decision tree model compares to the logistic regression model developed in Chapter 7, I have included the fit metrics for Logistic 1, the champion model from Chapter 7, in the same table. As shown, C&R Tree 2 outperforms Logistic 1, indicating some progress in improving predictive power. We will continue to explore additional models using other algorithms and compare their performance with these existing models.

Decision Tree Result Interpretation

Assuming the model fit is acceptable, the next step is to interpret the results of the decision tree. First, we need to understand the tree hierarchy and how each node contributes to predicting the target variable, which is whether a passenger recommends the airline. Figure 8.9 displays the full tree plot of our champion model. Notably, the tree contains 20 nodes (excluding Node 0) and 12 leaves.

305. I have extracted the top three nodes to illustrate the detailed information within each node and explain their significance (Figure 8.10). Each node typically consists of the following components:

  • Node ID

  • Statistics for all levels of the target variable within the sample, including:

    • The percentage of passengers who do not recommend the airline (NO).

    • The percentage of passengers who do recommend the airline (YES).

    • The total count of records in the sample for that node.

For example, in Figure 8.10, if we look at the node Personal Travel, we can interpret the following:

  • There are 15,826 records in the sample for passengers who travel for personal purposes.

  • 89.119% of these passengers do not recommend the airline.

  • Only 10.881% of these passengers do recommend the airline.

How to Interpret a Tree Plot

Tree plots can have many nodes and branches, which may seem confusing at first. Without a clear approach, it's easy to get lost in the structure and misinterpret the plot. The simplest way to explain and interpret a tree plot is to follow the hierarchy from top to bottom, tracing each branch.

In this example, I break the tree plot down by nodes and branches, following the natural hierarchy of the tree. I also create a bullet-point hierarchy that mirrors the tree structure. This method makes it easier to explain the outputs and reduces the chances of errors.

Tree Plot Interpretation

  • Travel Purpose—Personal travel: 89.12% do not recommend the airline; 10.88% recommend it.

    • Airline status—Blue, Gold, Platinum: 95.40% do not recommend the airline; 4.60% recommend it.

    • 306. Airline status—Silver: 55.11% do not recommend the airline; 44.89% recommend it.

      • Arrival delay—less than 5.5 minutes: 36.33% do not recommend the airline; 63.67% recommend it.

      • Arrival delay—5.5 minutes or more: 90.53% do not recommend the airline; 9.47% recommend it.

  • Travel Purpose—Business Travel & Mileage ticket: 29.86% do not recommend the airline; 70.14% recommend it.

    • Airline status—Blue, Platinum: 36.4% do not recommend the airline; 63.60% recommend it.

      • Arrival delay—less than 5.5 minutes: 29.66% do not recommend the airline; 70.34% recommend it.

        • Age—less than 63.5 years: 27.69% do not recommend the airline; 72.31% recommend it.

        • Age—63.5 years or more: 51.88% do not recommend the airline; 48.12% recommend it.

          • Average number of flights per year—26.78 flights or less: 46.49% do not recommend the airline; 53.51% recommend it.

          • Average number of flights per year—more than 26.78 flights: 60.77% do not recommend the airline; 39.23% recommend it.

        • Travel purpose—mileage tickets: 76.31% do not recommend the airline; 23.69% recommend it.

    • Airline status—Gold, Silver: 16.54% do not recommend the airline; 83.46% recommend it.

As you can see, it is not too hard if we make sure the bullet hierarchy matches the tree hierarchy. Typically, in data mining reports, we just need to present the tree plot and explain some key nodes and branches. There is no need to cover all nodes and branches because it could result in many pages of details. Nonetheless, I provide a full interpretation here as a demonstration so you can refer back to this page to learn how to interpret the tree plot.

You can also notice some nodes, such as age, travel purpose, or destination state, are presented multiple times in the tree. That selection is determined by the splitting algorithm to maximize the model fit. In the case of age, this node needs to be split multiple times because CART only uses the binary split.

Variable Importance

Another key output of a decision tree model is the variable importance chart, which displays the relative importance of the predictors in predicting the target variable. This importance is calculated using complex formulas involving the sum of squared errors, but I won’t delve into the mathematical 307. details here. What's important to understand is that this score reflects how crucial each predictor is in forecasting the target variable, with values ranging from 0 to 1. The closer the score is to 1, the more important the predictor.

This chart is valuable because it highlights which predictors are most significant in predicting the target variable and ranks them accordingly. Figure 8.11 shows the predictor importance chart for the champion model, C&R Tree 2.

The results indicate that travel purpose is the most important predictor, followed by airline status, age, and arrival delay. On the other hand, percent of flights with other airlines, shopping amount at the airport, and number of loyalty cards are the least important predictors. Any predictors not included in this list are considered insignificant, meaning they do not contribute to predicting the target variable (whether to recommend the airline).

Tree Size Differences Between Tree Algorithms

Before concluding this example, I want to highlight how tree plots differ based on the tree algorithms used. Below are the example tree plots for all four algorithms:

  • Figure 8.12: CART plot—skinny, long tree.

  • Figure 8.13: QUEST plot—skinny, long tree.

  • Figure 8.14: CHAID tree plot—large, short tree.

  • Figure 8.15: C5.0 tree plot—large, short tree.308.

309. As you can see, the CART and QUEST algorithms use binary splits, resulting in skinny but long trees. In contrast, the CHAID and C5.0 algorithms use multiple splits, producing short but very large trees.

In my opinion, smaller trees are easier to understand and interpret, especially when presenting and explaining the tree hierarchy. Additionally, large trees tend to raise concerns about overfitting, which is why pruning the trees is important.310.

Example: Association Model Using Decision Trees

311. In this example, we build decision tree models for the Boston housing dataset. The target variable is a continuous variable, Imv, representing the median home value in the Boston area. Since in SPSS Modeler only the CART and CHAID tree algorithms can handle continuous target variables, we will focus on building CART and CHAID tree for this dataset. (As noted earlier, the C5.0 and QUEST algorithms in SPSS Modeler are limited to categorical target variables.)

  • Dataset: Boston.sav

  • Target variable: Imv (continuous—median home value)

Starting Point

Having completed the key steps of data exploration, modification, and partitioning for this dataset in Chapter 7, we will not repeat them here. Instead, our focus will be on the modeling process. For detailed configurations and insights from those earlier steps, please refer to the previous chapters. As a result, we will start with the Partition node and move forward to build the models, as illustrated in the following diagram.

Modeling

You may recall that in the Boston housing project, after data imputation and modification, we created three datasets:

  • A dataset with missing values in the target field Imv.

  • A dataset with imputed data for the field Imv.

  • A dataset with normalized data.

Since all the missing values are in the target field, our goal is to determine whether the decision tree algorithms can handle these missing values effectively. Additionally, because all predictors are continuous, we aim to evaluate how well these algorithms manage skewed data. For each of the three datasets, we will apply both the CART and CHAID algorithms, resulting in a total of six tree models. I will use the default settings for these algorithms.

  • C&R Tree 1: Imputed, normalized dataset using the CART algorithm (default settings)

  • CHAID Tree 1: Imputed, normalized dataset using the CHAID algorithm (default settings)

  • C&R Tree 2: Imputed, non-normalized dataset using the CART algorithm (default settings)

  • CHAID Tree 2: Imputed, non-normalized dataset using the CHAID algorithm (default settings)

  • 312. C&R Tree 3: Original dataset (with missing values, non-normalized) using the CART algorithm (default settings)

  • CHAID Tree 3: Original dataset (with missing values, non-normalized) using the CHAID algorithm (default settings)

Follow the same steps as before to add and set up these trees. Your stream should resemble the one shown below.

Champion Model

Run all six tree models and use the Analysis node to extract the model fit metrics for each. For association models with continuous target variables, you can extract the following metrics directly from the Analysis node output:

  • Minimum error

  • Maximum error

  • Mean error

  • Mean absolute error (MAE)

  • Standard deviation

  • Linear correlation

Other metrics would need to be calculated separately by exporting the output datasets to Excel, which is a time-consuming process. Unlike other software, SPSS Modeler offers limited fit metrics for association models. For the purpose of model comparison, we will focus on MAE. While it doesn’t provide the full picture of model performance and is scale-dependent, it is sufficient for comparing models. As always, we will use the results from the testing sample to compare the models.

Table 8.8 presents the comparison results for the six models. Among the CART models, the one using the original dataset (C&R Tree 3) performs best. For the CHAID models, the one using imputed, normalized data (CHAID 1) performs best while the worst-performing CHAID model is the one using the original dataset.

To assess the validity of the champion model, additional model fit metrics need to be calculated. Follow the same steps outlined in Chapter 7 to export the output data of CHAID 1 to Excel for further analysis.

Follow the steps below to export the CHAID 1 output to Excel:

  5. Click Apply and Run.
